title: Now that Cardinals QB Jacoby Brissett has his new deal, can he now focus on his team?
summary: We all know that last year, during training camp for the Arizona Cardinals, Jacoby Brissett was brought in as an experienced QB to back up starter Kyler Murray. That was the plan. If Murray became injured, there would be experience and knowledge behind him. At the time of the signing, Brissett (6’-4”, 235 pounds) had […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - JULY 28: Jacoby Brissett #7 of the Arizona Cardinals participates in a team practice ahead of the NFL season at State Farm Stadium on July 28, 2026 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images We all know that last year, during training camp for the Arizona Cardinals, Jacoby Brissett was brought in as an experienced QB to back up starter Kyler Murray. That was the plan. If Murray became injured, there would be experience and knowledge behind him. At the time of the signing, Brissett (6’-4”, 235 pounds) had nine years in the league and had played in 87 NFL games with 53 starts. RELATED: CARDINALS GIVE BRISSETT HIS RAISE However, he was considered a career backup. He did start two seasons while with the Indianapolis Colts back in 2019 and 2020. And he started the first 11 games of the 2022 season for the Cleveland Browns while their new quarterback, Deshaun Watson, was serving a league suspension. But on the remaining contracts with the five NFL clubs he was a roster member of, he was the team’s backup option. Even in 2024, when he was named the starter for the New England Patriots in Week 1, after just five starts, he was replaced by rookie Drake Maye. So, when he signed that two-year deal for $12.5 million during the 2025 free agency period, he was penciled in as Murray’s backup with Clayton Tune set as QB3. No drama, no quarterback competition, no worries. Except Murray became injured in the Tennessee Titans loss and was placed on IR. His practice window came up, and the team just kept him there as the offense had come alive with Brissett at the helm despite not winning games. Then Murray was released after Jonathan Gannon was fired and Mike LaFleur became the head coach, and a decision was made. Whether it was LaFleur or GM Monti Ossenfort who officially pulled the trigger to let Murray seek employment elsewhere, what remained was that Brissett was in line to become the starter for 2026. The #AZCardinals and veteran QB Jacoby Brissett have reached a deal to increase his compensation for 2026, as its new one year worth $15.5M with a chance to get $21M. AZ’s starter is now locked, already having begun practicing. pic.twitter.com/LwnQqqupIX — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) July 26, 2026 And after he was told he was the starter going forward, he wanted more money than an NFL starting QB should be getting, and not backup funds. And he got a pay bump for $15.5 million with incentives that could raise it to $21 million. Which, in NFL circles, is less than half the price that most league starters are getting. Of course, Brissett will turn 34 years old this season. He has been in the league 10 years and has had few opportunities to be considered any team’s starting quarterback. Brissett joined guys like Colt McCoy, Marcus Mariota, Blake Bortles, Case Keenum, Josh Dobbs, Kenny Pickett, Gardner Minshew, and Josh Johnson, who were all considered career backups. But now Brissett has his shiny new deal and is listed on the Cardinals’ first official depth chart as this year’s starting quarterback. Getting back to work With Brissett’s new contract signed, he started showing up for what he was being paid to be: Arizona’s leader on offense. He was set to make $1.5 million as the starting QB for one of 32 NFL clubs. He then showed up to work out in the Cardinals’ first training camp practice. Now, for the hard part. By hiring LaFleur, this meant installing a brand-new offense similar to what the Los Angeles Rams, San Francisco 49ers, and Green Bay Packers operate under. Brissett suddenly needed to learn the Cardinals’ playbook cover to cover. Not that he had not even cracked it open yet. But he missed out on all of the class meetings and practice sessions, which are extensions of the playbook. LaFleur took his time with Brissett. He penciled him in at the back of the line with practice reps, basically labeling him QB4. After a few practices, he finally got his first-team reps on a Sunday with LaFleur calling all the plays. The scheme is new, as is the system, so there was plenty to learn, mistakes to learn from, and finally become comfortable with. Brissett told ESPN Arizona : “Obviously, after this night of sleep that I do get, I’ll go back to three hours of sleep for work purposes now. So, I’m not naive to understand that it’s still a lot of work to be done.” Getting up to speed on a newly installed offense isn’t as simple as changing out the battery in your vehicle. It’s like installing a new starter. In some vehicles, it is easy to get to with comfortable access. Whereas in others, things need to be removed just to get to the starter’s bolts. Most of the Europeans vehicles, you can barely get a hand in a crevice to reach it. Some are buried deep inside the engine valley under the intake manifold. The Audi S4 houses the starter unit directly through or inside the engine mount assembly. The point is, each NFL offense is different. But Brissett has been forced to catch on with many offenses with the five teams he has been hired by, with six different offenses since he was with the Patriots twice. This is just another offense to learn. Brissett explained: “I think that’s what gave me even more confidence in myself is knowing that I’ve been through so many different phases of this thing of football that I knew once the business got handled. Now, the football is the football. I know I’ll take care of that. And I had no doubt that I’m going to put the work in.” Which comes at the right time. Veteran Minshew and the rookie Carson Beck have been at every OTA and minicamp. They have attended each class session. Both have been practicing and receiving tutelage this entire time. And each showed flashes that they could run this team come Week 1. Beck has been seen early to late at the practice facility since being selected in the third round of April’s NFL draft. So, he and Minshew have a leg up on learning this new offense. Brissett understood that without actually participating in team activities, he was getting behind: “I think that’s the reason why we did get a deal done because they knew I would get the work done, and I think my teammates understood that. And obviously Coach LaFleur doesn’t know me as well, but somebody told him that I’ll do the work.” Carson Beck is about to tell Jacoby Brissett to take your pay raise and get comfortable on the bench if this keeps up in the preseason https://t.co/r48YRWkGby — Ron Carthen (@rcarthen) August 7, 2026 And while Minshew is perfectly capable of running an offense, it is Beck who is getting the most attention. Especially since he balled out during the Hall of Fame Game. Yes, Beck played with the second-string against the Carolina Panthers’ second-team defense. We get that and can easily place these facts in perspective. A lot of new working parts Playing well and having talent are one thing. What Beck showed in the team’s first exhibition game was that he understood this new offense. He might not have everything down pat, but by golly, he certainly displayed that he was fully grasping what LaFleur is teaching and wanting from his quarterback. After all, this year’s new offense has proven to be a winning system. The Rams, 49ers, and Packers were all playoff clubs last year. With basically this same offense. What these teams execute on that side of the ball is what Arizona will now be doing. And the Cardinals have the offensive weapons while simultaneously attempting to revamp the offensive line. All they need is a capable quarterback. Is that Brissett? He admitted that during his time off from the team activities, he hadn’t been completely through the playbook but had an overall idea of the general base. He didn’t state that he filled his days playing the latest version of “Call of Duty,” but that he will start to digest the wrinkles of the scheme as each page of the playbook is turned. Brissett added: “ I got a long way to go. I mean, I’m willing to put the work in. But it’s…

title: Atlanta Falcons training camp 2026: Day 9 news, notes, injuries, and updates
summary: BUFORD, Ga. — The Falcons found themselves back under the Georgia summer lights, with one of their most anticipated practices of training camp coming at Buford’s Lanier High School. The practice start time was at 7:00 p.m. with the pads out and a presumed tackling period also in store. Unfortunately, Mother Nature had other plans […]
full_text: BUFORD, Ga. — The Falcons found themselves back under the Georgia summer lights, with one of their most anticipated practices of training camp coming at Buford’s Lanier High School. The practice start time was at 7:00 p.m. with the pads out and a presumed tackling period also in store. Unfortunately, Mother Nature had other plans as the session was abruptly brought to an end at around 8:10 p.m. after a lightning strike was observed in the area, before any tackling took place and in the midst of what was an exciting day of 11-on-11s. This was much to the disappointment of the capacity crowd which filed into the Lanier Longhorns’ bleachers. Excitement for the season is mounting, as it always is at this time of year, and the team did treat the fans to an intriguing hour or so of practice nonetheless. An alternate view https://t.co/jP7w6r7AyB pic.twitter.com/qxSKGAybcY — Adnan Ikic (@SayWhichWay) August 8, 2026 Below are my news and notes from Day 9 of Falcons’ 2026 Training Camp, at Lanier High School. Injury Updates Safety Jessie Bates III remained out. It was stated previously that he is dealing with a back ailment which has now cost him a fourth straight day of practice. S DeMarcco Hellams got most of the work with the first team in his place. DL Zach Harrison was activated and cleared to return to practice, so there is some good news on the injury font. RT Jawaan Taylor remains out, on the PUP list, and RT Wanya Morris was still out as well. T Michael Jarrel continued getting most of the first team reps at right tackle, and I saw T/G Ethan Onianwa and T/G Kem Dewberry rotated in with the first team some as well. Taylor was right in front of me at the beginning of the night, and it was interesting to note that he was wearing a full leg sleeve (his injury is listed as an elbow/triceps). Tua Tagovailoa Shines in 11s QB Tua Tagovailoa seems to be fully back and in the swing of things after missing the first few days of camp, and getting worked back in over the next few. He took all of the first team reps in 11-on-11 periods, and looked pretty good. Overall, the former national champion with the University of Alabama went 6-8 in these scrimmage periods, including 2-3 during an early red zone portion inside the 10, throwing touchdowns to WR Jahan Dotson and WR Drake London (who operated out of the slot on this particular play). His best throw of the day came on a layered pass which traveled over 35 yards in the air and landed in the hands of WR Olamide Zaccheaus off a well established play action where the protection held up. London and Dotson each were recipients of throws which came in the full field portion of 11-on-11 in addition to their red zone looks, making both the only players who caught multiple passes with the first team. TE Kyle Pitts on a short catch was the other recipient of a Tagovailoa completion. I was also impressed with how effectively London was schemed open on his second completion, where he ran what looked like a drag route from right to left and was left without a defender within 15 yards of his vicinity amidst the chaos of the play, gaining some real chunk yardage in the immediate aftermath. Bijan Robinson makes the crowd erupt After his brief “hold in” which resulted in his briefly becoming the highest paid running back in the NFL (until Jahmyr Gibbs’ extension a few days later), RB Bijan Robinson also seems to be getting his footing under him with each passing day. Following a rough first play of 11s where he was motioning from the left for what looked like an end around play with the quarterback operating out of the shotgun, Bijan had the handoff from Tua botched which resulted in a fumble. That, however, was not a tone setter as both players bounced back rather quickly. Namely, the first play in which Robinson successfully touched the ball — a toss play to the left out of the shotgun — he found an open hole in the defense, turned the corner and made a move in the open field which freed him up for a 55-yard touchdown run. The capacity crowd was the loudest of the night on this play as the former Texas Longhorns running back poetically scored on a field whose logo imitates that of his alma mater. Robinson had a later play, on an identical toss to the left out of the shotgun, where he once again managed to turn the corner for a pretty decent gain as his shiftiness in the open field remains the team’s most dangerous offensive threat. Young defensive lineman have their moments While the first team offense had a strong day overall, the defense was not without some of their own victories. Tagovailoa wound up taking a couple of sacks, and the first one came courtesy of DT Brandon Dorlus , who has gotten to the quarterback multiple times already throughout the course of this camp. Dorlus, who broke out with 8.5 sacks a year ago, will be one of the key cogs of this defensive line going into his third year in the league. DT Maason Smith , who was acquired in a trade with the Jacksonville Jaguars for DT Ruke Orhorhoro , had his standout moments as well. He had a big push up the middle which caved in the offensive line and resulted in the second sack of Tua, and earlier in the night he beat C Ryan Neuzil in a one on one drill pitting offensive lineman against their defensive counterparts before scrimmages began. Nobody was more impressive in that particular drill (which the offensive lineman mostly dominated) than EDGE James Pearce Jr. who somehow got around Michael Jarrel without even being touched on a speed move on his first rep, before handily beating T Brandon Walton on his next rep. Pearce got more work with the first team defense today after spending time exclusively with the second team early on in camp. Other Notes K Nick Folk remained automatic, as the team started the evening with some field goal drills. The veteran free agent signing kicked in at least three field goals, and maybe even more that I just missed seeing because they sent him out there before the official start time, drilling one from 50+ as a long. As far as I know, he has missed just one kick in all of camp, and that was on a play where he slipped. LB Kendal Daniels and LB Harold Perkins both rotated in with the first team once again. It seems that the rookies will be tasked with making an immediate impact on the Falcons’ defense this year. While Bijan was the main headliner, the “other” B. Robinson also had a strong day. RB Brian Robinson Jr. rotated in with the first team on a red zone play inside the 5-yard-line and punched it in for a touchdown before scampering for a 20-yard rushing touchdown after making a defender miss on his very next touch, with the second team. RB Nathan Carter had his own score from a red zone snap, as he continues to lead the pack in that RB3 competition. The second team defense mostly got the better of their counterparts, led by QB Jack Strand and QB Cooper Rush . Rush did not complete a single pass in 11-on-11 and Strand’s lone moment of the day came on an early touchdown strike from inside the 5-yard-line to WR Vinny Anthony before he was stifled as well. The Falcons had some moments of some creativity and trickery in this practice. In the middle of field goal drills, they had a snap where instead of the next Folk kick they broke into a half speed fake field goal where P Jake Bailey threw a touchdown pass to C Corey Levin (the defense, which was in position, did not attempt to stop or break up the pass as everyone was moving in a jog). The most unique play came with the second team out there, where they ran a type of “Philly Special” which involved Carter taking a toss and then handing the ball off to Dotson, who targeted Jack Strand near the sideline about 20 yards downfield (the pass fell incomplete, however). QB Michael Penix Jr. did not get any work outside of some warm up throws. The coaching staff has in the past given him his own 7-on-7 period at the end of practice to get some work in. Whether that was part of the plan…

title: Mercedes-Benz Stadium Nominated for Best NFL Stadium and Best NFL Stadium Food
summary: USA Today has released its USA Today Readers’ Choice Awards in the world of sports, and it has 12 different categories:  For all of the college football fans, you can scour the other nine college-related polls, and if you’re feeling quite…strong…about your tailgating vehicle, there’s a poll for that as well.  However, the polls that […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - JULY 15: A general view shows the exterior of Atlanta Stadium prior to the FIFA World Cup 2026 Semi Final match between England and Argentina on July 15, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Liu Lu/VCG via Getty Images) | VCG via Getty Images USA Today has released its USA Today Readers’ Choice Awards in the world of sports, and it has 12 different categories: Best College Sports Town Best College for Sports Fans Best College Sports Tradition Best College Fight Song Best College Mascot Best College Marching Band Best College Walk-Out Tradition Best College Football Stadium Best College Tailgating Experience Best NFL Stadium Best NFL Stadium Food Best Vehicle for Tailgating For all of the college football fans, you can scour the other nine college-related polls, and if you’re feeling quite…strong…about your tailgating vehicle, there’s a poll for that as well. However, the polls that we are worried about today are the Best NFL Stadium and Best NFL Stadium food, where Mercedes-Benz Stadium, home of the Atlanta Falcons , has been nominated in both categories. Vote Mercedes-Benz Stadium for Best NFL Stadium It’s unique, everything is new, the concession prices are fan friendly. But when it comes to amenities, there are so many great options that fans tend to spend time enjoying the stadium away from their seats. It’s a world-class venue. Vote Mercedes-Benz Stadium for Best NFL Stadium Food Across the league, very little about the dining experience can be considered fan friendly. Mercedes-Benz Stadium is the obvious exception. At Falcons games, you can get an entire spread of food for $20. It’s a great concept that more teams should adopt. You can vote daily for Mercedes-Benz Stadium until Monday, August 10th!

title: Buffalo Bills 53-man roster projection: Post training camp
summary: The Buffalo Bills are home in Orchard Park after a short but active training camp at St. John Fisher University, which means it’s time for a 53-man roster projection. While there weren’t a litany of enormous personnel developments during the team’s time in Pittsford, some alterations from my post-draft projection are needed… Quarterback (2) Kyle […]
full_text: ROCHESTER, NEW YORK - JULY 29: T.J. Sanders #98 talks with Michael Hoecht #55 of the Buffalo Bills during training camp at St. John Fisher University on July 29, 2026 in Rochester, New York. (Photo by Joe Hrycych/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills are home in Orchard Park after a short but active training camp at St. John Fisher University, which means it’s time for a 53-man roster projection. While there weren’t a litany of enormous personnel developments during the team’s time in Pittsford, some alterations from my post-draft projection are needed… Quarterback (2) Josh Allen Shane Buechele Kyle Allen underwhelmed at training camp almost every day. Buechele came on strong late. I think we have a serious QB2 battle on our hands this preseason. Running Back (3) James Cook Ray Davis Ty Johnson Johnson hurt his leg in the Return of the Blue and Red Scrimmage, but it shouldn’t change the numbers game at the running back position for the start of the season. Wide Receiver (7) D.J. Moore Khalil Shakir Josh Palmer Keon Coleman Skyler Bell Mecole Hardman Trent Sherfield Going with seven — instead of what was the traditional six — because this is Joe Brady’s team now, and I assume he’s going to want to pass it and pass it often. Hardman looked as spry as ever at camp, made some plays down the field, and can serve as the club’s primary returner. Sherfield makes it on special teams availability. Tight End (3) Dalton Kincaid Dawson Knox Jackson Hawes I’ll focus on Hawes here — he played 43% of the offensive snaps as a rookie and turned in a damn good first season in the NFL, particularly for a fifth-round pick. There’s untapped receiving potential in Hawes, and he absolutely has the game to be the stand-in for the departed Reggie Gilliam as a lead-blocking fullback when needed. Offensive Line (9) Dion Dawkins Alec Anderson Connor McGovern O’Cyrus Torrence Spencer Brown Austin Corbett Sedrick Van Pran-Granger Tylan Grable Jude Bowry Notable-ish cuts are to Lloyd Cushenberry and 2025 seventh-round pick Chase Lundt. While it’s not particularly easy to glean observations from the sidelines at camp, I did not notice nor talk to anyone who mentioned noteworthy positives from either of those two at St. John Fisher. Corbett and SVPG are the two swing interior blockers. Grable steps into the old Alec Anderson/David Edwards swing tackle role. Defensive Line (7) Ed Oliver Deone Walker T.J. Sanders Phidarian Mathis DeWayne Carter Landon Jackson Zane Durant Pretty cut and dry here — and Carter showed a glimmer of promise at times during training camp, even at his beefed up size. Inside Linebacker (4) Terrel Bernard Kaleb Elarms-Orr Dorian Williams Keonta Jenkins I, personally, don’t believe Sean McDermott was a big Dorian Williams guy. But we don’t know how Jim Leonard views him. He may love his fiery style on the field. Having said that, I believe KEO did enough at camp to earn a Week 1 starting role. Run defense, screen IDing, downfield coverage. It was all there. Joe Andreessen is the odd-man out as of now, although he should get plenty of run in the preseason to work his magic like he’s done in August each of the last two years. Rush Linebacker (5) Greg Rousseau Bradley Chubb Michael Hoecht T.J. Parker Javon Solomon One more rush linebacker from my post-draft projection, as Hoecht has made a magnificently fast return to the field after his early November injury. He was explosive, and reasonably disruptive at camp. The same goes for Solomon, who sneaks onto the roster as a player Leonhard may grow to love as a situation stand-up rusher. Defensive Backs (10) * Christian Benford Maxwell Hairston Dee Alford Davison Igbinosun Cole Bishop CJ Gardner-Johnson Jordan Hancock Damar Hamlin Jalon Kilgore Sam Franklin Jr. The only change here that represents any semblance of surpise would be Hamlin over Geno Stone. I saw a reinvigorated Hamlin at camp. Simply more plays out of him there, heading into the preseason. Franklin Jr. even had practices with the first-team group during CJGJ’s short injury absence, and he’s an animal as a gunner on the punt team. Also, don’t be surprised if Kilgore is on the field in sub packages as a rookie. If it weren’t for the sensational camp from KEO, the former South Carolina safety would be drawing all the headlines as the most impressive Bills rookie in Rochester. And no Kani Walker… yet. title: First impressions of Buffalo Bills’ new Highmark Stadium
summary: What an evening inside the new Highmark Stadium for the Return of the Blue and Red Scrimmage on Saturday night for Buffalo Bills fans. I was fortunate enough to be one of the 51,807 in attendance for the first full-scale event inside the Bills’ new building, and below are my first impressions along with reviews […]
full_text: What an evening inside the new Highmark Stadium for the Return of the Blue and Red Scrimmage on Saturday night for Buffalo Bills fans. I was fortunate enough to be one of the 51,807 in attendance for the first full-scale event inside the Bills’ new building, and below are my first impressions along with reviews from a collection of Bills fans I talked to after the festivities. Concourses inside new Highmark Stadium Because everyone first enters the stadium into a concourse — and the old stadium’s concourses were narrow concrete hallways — this is everyone’s first impression of the stadium. I was thoroughly impressed by how expansive they are, and the 360 degree view of the field provides serious Major League Baseball vibes. Once you’re in the stadium, you can see the field from the concourse regardless of what level you’re on. That’s an amazing touch, and the first and probably most sizable of many significant upgrades in this new stadium compared to the Bills’ old digs. Concession spots in new Highmark Stadium It feels necessary to go here next, because when you’re in the concourses you’re inundated with spots to get food and drink. The opposite was true at the old stadium, where it was clear the Bills were far behind the rest of the NFL in terms of amount of concession locations within the building. That led to unreasonably long lines at any part of the game. Said lines often spanned the entire width of the concourses, which created incredibly congested walkways for anyone attempting to find a bathroom during halftime or between drives. In this new stadium, the concessions options feel endless. They’re everywhere. And, vitally, many of them are dug into the wall of the outer rim of the concourse, so you if there are lines, they won’t protrude into the main walkway. Also, the main concession stands named after Buffalo neighborhoods are a tasteful element to this stadium. Food inside new Highmark Stadium Natural segue here — the food options inside the Bills stadium are un-be-lievable. Night and day difference from the minimal variety offered in the old building. And it’s all local, essentially. While the wings and pizza aren’t from a Buffalo staple, you’re offered Beef on Weck using Wegmans rolls, a plethora of options from Texas BBQ-Indian fusion restaurant Southern Junction — a multiple James Beard Award nominee — Babcia’s Pierogi, Anderson’s Ice Cream and many more. I love that. Also, don’t worry about waiting 20 minutes for your wings to fry. Wings along with most of the menu items — like chicken fingers, burgers, and fries — are all pre-made and under serious heat lamps. I got wings on my way out and they were legitimately hot (temperature wise), and slathered in rich Buffalo sauce. I didn’t have high expectations for wings being made at such a large scale, but they were rock solid. My wife and kids had the soft serve ice cream, and at 7 and 9 years old, my daughters are ice cream experts. They insatntly raved about it and it was the first topic of conversation this morning. Regarding drinks — the options are basically endless. In many of the enormous grab-and-go fridges were not only the staple beer and seltzer brands but many beverages I’d never heard of with a multitude of flavors. You will be able to snag your drink much faster in this new stadium and you will be overwhelmed with choices before you’re miffed there aren’t enough. Signage inside new Highmark Stadium This is one area I felt was a bit underwhelming. Or in this case, confusing. There weren’t enough large signs directing you to your seats or identifying where bathrooms were. Many of the doors only had small, office-building like signs next to them, and it wasn’t super clear how to find escalators and elevators. However, I did realize some of the branded congregating spots around the stadium like the Charge Bar and Labatt Blue Zone are simply just not familiar to anyone yet, meaning signs with directing you toward any of them may take a while to become landmarks for you and your family and friends. Sightlines inside the new Highmark Stadium The seat architecture in the Bills new home is magnificent. They’ll managed to place seats closer and lower to the field The open feel of the concourses are awesome. The intimacy of the seats are foundational elements of this building. My dad and I had front row 300 level seats on the visitor side 40 yard line in the old stadium. I’ve always been incredibly grateful to have seats with that vantage point. For as great as those seats were, there’s no doubt we were really far away from the field. When I got to those same seats in this new stadium, I was blown away at how low and close to the field they were. The vantage point shifted to what I’d estimate was like the back rows of the 100s or 200s in the old stadium. And it felt like I could toss a football onto the field from my seats, when that was never the case in the seats across the street. Even the 400 level directly behind us are impossibly close to the field for being an upper deck of a modern NFL stadium. While upon first glance, every seat looked to provide a glorious vantage point — that was much closer to the field than the previous stadium — I’ve since learned that’s not exactly true. Some seats — not many — have partially obstructed views from the entirety of the field, like this once sent in by Garrett (a fellow Rumbler). Pretty strange that oversight exists inside the new stadium but I’m assuming these obstructions were necessary evils given the stacked nature of each level. Video boards and noise inside new Highmark Stadium The video boards are small by new-stadium standards. No doubt. We were told that was done on purpose, because if you’re physically at the game, you’re attention will likely be on the field, not a screen. I 100% agree with that priniciple. The money saved from not splurging on expansive Jumbotrons was spent on ridiculous, state-of-the-art sound system. And the acoustics from the canopy made all the music and fan reactions stupid loud. I’m guessing the new Highmark Stadium will quickly be regarded as one of the loudest stadiums in football, providing the Bills the home-field advantage every team wants from its fans and building. Anything else you’re wondering about the new stadium? Do you have thoughts of your own? Drop a comment to start a conversation.

title: Bills news: Recapping Return of the Blue & Red
summary: The Buffalo Bills’ first public event inside their new, state-of-the-art Highmark Stadium occurred Saturday night, when the team did drills and held an inter-squad scrimmage during their annual Return of the Blue & Red practice. full_text: The bison sculptures sit in Family Circle outside Highmark Stadium home to the Buffalo Bills on Thursday, July 23, 2026.(Harry Scull Jr./Buffalo News via Getty Images) The Buffalo Bills’ first public event inside their new, state-of-the-art Highmark Stadium occurred Saturday night, when the team did drills and held an inter-squad scrimmage during their annual Return of the Blue & Red practice. More than 51,000 Bills fans took advantage of their first chance to see the Bills’ new stadium in person, and today’s edition of Buffalo Rumblinks leads off with news and observations from the Return of the Blue & Red practice, a night that featured plenty of fireworks—including terrific touchdown tosses from Josh Allen to Khalil Shakir and Allen to DJ Moore during the scrimmage portion—both on and off the field. Were you among the Bills Mafia members in attendance? Check out the assessments and then be sure to leave your thoughts on the new stadium experience in the comments section. Fans get first look at new Highmark Stadium On a night filled with plenty of excitement, it was Jim Leonhard’s defense that came up with the biggest splash plays early on. Making his new Highmark Stadium “debut,” Josh Allen was picked off by Buffalo’s defense four times, with Cole Bishop, Christian Benford, Damar Hamlin and Dee Alford coming away with interceptions of the former NFL MVP. But Allen bounced back nicely and closed off the night with some phenomenal throws, including a picture-perfect dart to DJ Moore that went for 35 yards, a laser beam on a deep throw to Khalil Shakir for a TD, and a nifty TD toss to Dawson Knox late in the practice. Who else stood out? Cole Bishop, defensive back Jordan Hancock, and nickel corner Dee Alford made several big plays; Tyler Bass was a perfect 8-for-8 on field goal tries; running back James Cook rattled off a few big runs going up against Buffalo’s starting defense; defensive tackle Deone Walker disrupted a few plays along the line of scrimmage; and running back Ty Johnson and center Connor McGovern suffered apparent leg injuries and had to leave practice. title: Every Buffalo Bills offensive guard contract handled by Brandon Beane
summary: The Buffalo Bills dominated NFL headlines on Friday, August 7 in signing right guard O’Cyrus Torrence to a massive contract extension. Torrence’s new deal will pay him $78.4 million, including $46 million guaranteed over the course of four years, beginning with the 2027 NFL season. It’s certainly true that Torrence’s latest contract is set to […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - NOVEMBER 20: O'Cyrus Torrence #64 of the Buffalo Bills drops back to block during an NFL football game against the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium on November 20, 2025 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills dominated NFL headlines on Friday, August 7 in signing right guard O’Cyrus Torrence to a massive contract extension. Torrence’s new deal will pay him $78.4 million, including $46 million guaranteed over the course of four years, beginning with the 2027 NFL season. It’s certainly true that Torrence’s latest contract is set to carry massive cap weight against Buffalo’s salary cap, adding to an already astronomically priced offensive line. It’s also an immediate point of contention for people who aren’t fully versed in the role of an offensive guard, as well those quick to pass judgment on the recently promoted president of football operations/general manager Brandon Beane. This latest deal is far from the first offensive guard contract that Beane has signed during his time at One Bills Drive. How do others Bills contracts at the position during his tenure stack up? Let’s take a quick stroll down memory lane, a path paved with plenty of hyperlinks leading to the archives of Buffalo Rumblings. Vladimir Ducasse Buffalo signed offensive guard Vladimir Ducasse to a three-year, $3.5 million free-agent contract ahead of the 2017 NFL season. Ducasse started 12 games (after spending the first 4 weeks inactive) in his first season with Buffalo . After making nine starts to begin the 2018 season, Ducasse was benched in favor of rookie offensive guard Wyatt Teller . Ducasse was released in August of 2019 . During two seasons with the Bills, Ducasse made 21 regular-season starts (22 games played), adding one playoff start in 2017. Wyatt Teller Wyatt Teller’s history with the Bills is fraught fan angst. Buffalo originally selected Wyatt Teller 166th overall (Round 5) during the 2018 NFL Draft . Teller would only last one season with the Bills after signing his rookie deal, starting seven games in eight total appearances . Days prior to the start of the 2019 NFL regular season, Beane traded Teller (and a 2021 seventh-round pick) to the Cleveland Browns in exchange for a pair of picks (fifth- and sixth-round) in the 2020 NFL Draft. Teller went on to a stellar seven-season tenure with the Browns. Cody Ford Selected by Buffalo in Round 2 (38th overall) of the 2019 NFL Draft , Ford signed his four-year rookie deal and spent the entirety of that first season playing right tackle . In that season’s playoff race, Ford was fined more than $28,000 for a blindside block in a game against the Houston Texans. It was a play that garnered plenty of controversy , and one that was ultimately levied as a reduced fine of $4,000 for Ford. Ford succeeded Spain at left guard in 2020, making seven starts in the regular season , though ultimately benched in favor of Ike Boettger and then later Ryan Bates. The trouble with Ford was his and the team’s inability to nail down a starting spot for long anywhere along the offensive line. In 2021, Ford moved over to right guard and made seven starts in 15 games played . Ahead of the 2022 NFL season, Ford was traded to the Arizona Cardinals in return for a 2023 fifth-round pick. Ike Boettger Offensive lineman Ike Boettger entered the NFL as an undrafted free agent, signing a three-year, $1,71 million deal with Buffalo following the 2018 NFL Draft. After being waived ahead of Week 1 that season, Boettger was claimed by the Kansas City Chiefs. Boettger made his way back to the Bills following his release from KC later that month, and he went on to play in six games at offensive tackle over the next two seasons. Buffalo tendered (as a restricted free agent/RFA) then re-signed Boettger to a one-year RFA deal for the 2021 NFL season. Boettger made 10 regular-season starts (15 games played) at left guard during the 2021 season before a torn Achilles claimed the remainder of his season. He re-signed on a one-year, $$1,047,500 million deal with the Bills for the 2022 NFL season, but spent majority of the campaign on Buffalo’s reserve/physically unable to perform (PUP) list as a result of that late-season Achilles injury. The Bills signed Boettger to another one-year contract ($1,182,500 ) for the 2023 NFL season , ultimately releasing him at final cutdowns ahead of Week 1. Jon Feliciano Offensive guard Jon Feliciano originally arrived in Buffalo in 2019 as a free agent on a two-year, $8.3 million deal that included $2.4 million guaranteed . Beane later re-signed Jon Feliciano to a three-year, $17 million contract . In three seasons with the Bills, Feliciano started 31 of 34 regular-season games, adding four playoff starts among six total postseason games. Buffalo eventually released Feliciano ahead of the 2022 NFL season . Spencer Long The Bills signed offensive guard Spencer Long to a three-year, $12.6 million contract early in 2019. The team picked up his second-year option for the 2020 NFL season, ultimately releasing him during training camp later that summer. Long announced his retirement from the NFL two weeks later. Quinton Spain After playing out his four-year, undrafted rookie free-agent (UDFA) contract with the Tennessee Titans, Quinton Spain signed a one-year free-agent contract to play for the Bills during the 2019 NFL season. Following a promising season playing every offensive snap in which he didn’t give up a sack, Spain was rewarded with a three-year, $15 million contract extension ahead of the 2020 NFL season. It was a contract that failed to meet expectations, with Spain starting at left guard only for Weeks 1 and 2 before being benched in favor of Cody Ford and later Brian Winters. Ryan Bates At the close of training camp in 2019, Buffalo made a trade with the Philadelphia Eagles that sent defensive end Eli Harold to Philly to acquire versatile undrafted rookie offensive guard Ryan Bates. Though Bates’ rookie contract was initiated by the Eagles’ front office, he never played a snap with the team. As a rookie, Bates did appear in eight regular-season games and three postseason contests with Buffalo. Bates would go on to play out his rookie contract with the Bills, starting four games in 41 games played over three seasons. Buffalo tendered Bates , a restricted free agent following his UDFA rookie deal, ahead of free agency in 2022. Bates would pay visits to the Minnesota Vikings and New England Patriots before meeting with and signing an offer sheet to play for the Chicago Bears during the 2022 season. We soon learned that Beane decided to match the Bears’ offer to Bates, signing him to a four-year, $17 million deal with the first two years fully guaranteed to the tune of $8.85 million . Bates would go on to play two more seasons with the Bills, starting 15 regular-season games and two playoff matchups in 2022; then appearing in 17 regular-season and two playoff games in 2023. Beane then decided to trade Bates to Chicago in March of 2024 , receiving a fifth-round pick in the 2024 NFL Draft in return. In five seasons with Buffalo, Bates made 19 starts in 73 regular-season games for the Bills, adding four starts in nine playoff games. Brian Winters The Bills signed offensive guard Brian Winters to a one-year, $3 million contract ($2 million guaranteed) ahead of the 2020 NFL season. In one season with Buffalo, Before being benched ahead of a Monday Night Football game late in 2020, Winters started nine regular-season games (16 total), adding in three playoff appearances. Winters signed a contract to play for the Arizona Cardinals after his lone season with the Bills. Daryl Williams A former fourth-round pick of the Carolina Panthers, offensive lineman Daryl Williams signed a one-year, $2.5 million contract to play in Buffalo during the 2020 season. That first year he started at right tackle in every game for the team, including 16 regular-season games, plus three playoff…

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 35 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - DECEMBER 24: Brian Burns #0 of the Carolina Panthers readies for the play during the second half of the game against the Green Bay Packers at Bank of America Stadium on December 24, 2023 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #35. Brian Burns I’m sure this one is going to get the people going. Throughout most of Carolina Panthers history, the team was known for having a formidable pass rush. From the early days with Kevin Greene and Lamar Lathon, to the first Super Bowl team with Julius Peppers and Mike Rucker, to the second Super Bowl team with Charles Johnson and Kawann Short, there’s almost always been someone along the line that instilled fear in opposing offensive coordinators. That hasn’t really been the case in recent times, save for one player—Brian Burns. The Panthers drafted Burns in the first round of the 2019 draft, and he was a welcome addition to a team that had been counting on an aging Mario Addison and an aging Julius Peppers for sack production. He immediately contributed in a rotational role as a rookie, contributing 7.5 sacks. He would follow that with consistent production from a sack perspective and elite production according to some advanced metrics. The discrepancy between the elite advanced metrics and the just-good traditional counting stats became the story of Burns’ time in Carolina. In his five years as a Panther, he averaged just over 9 sacks per season, which is good, but he frequently graded out as one of the most disruptive pass rushers. He was often the victim of his poor supporting cast, as he’d be the only player able to generate pressure, which allowed easy escape lanes for opposing quarterbacks, diminishing his raw sack totals. Burns seemingly wanted to be paid as one of the league’s elite pass rushers, but the Panthers were hesitant to pay him that way. They still held onto him through the end of his rookie contract and franchise tagged him before ultimately trading him away for pennies on the dollar to the New York Giants. He just finished an all pro season after finishing second in the league with 16.5 sacks. Public opinion soured on Burns later in his Panthers tenure, in part because of frustration over the sack production and probably in part because of some pre-coping with his imminent departure. But the Panthers have struggled to replicate anything like Burns’ production in the two years since he left, and it’d be mighty nice to have a player of his caliber on the line. Burns won’t go down as one of the most beloved Panthers of all time, but his talent was undeniable. It’s unfortunate that we never really got to see how he contribute to a Panthers team that was actually competitive. Still, he did enough to earn spot number 35 on the list of top 100 Panthers of all time.

title: Bears WR Luther Burden III to miss a month with groin injury, Week 1 return possible
summary: Bears wide receiver Luther Burden III is expected to miss about a month due to the groin injury he suffered in practice on Saturday, Matt Zenitz of CBS Sports reported on Sunday. The hope within the organization, according to Zenitz, is that Burden will be ready for the Bears’ Week 1 matchup against the Panthers […]
full_text: Bears wide receiver Luther Burden III is expected to miss about a month due to the groin injury he suffered in practice on Saturday, Matt Zenitz of CBS Sports reported on Sunday. The hope within the organization, according to Zenitz, is that Burden will be ready for the Bears’ Week 1 matchup against the Panthers on Sep. 13. A previous report from NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport indicated that Burden would miss time, though no clear timetable was given. In this anticipated span, Burden would miss the entirety of the preseason, as well as the rest of training camp. That said, it doesn’t appear that he would miss much of the regular season due to the injury, if he misses any time at all. Burden, 22, put together an impressive rookie campaign in 2025. The second-round pick out of Missouri finished the year with 47 catches for 652 yards and two touchdowns. He was particularly efficient in the second half of the season; his 17-game pace from Week 10 onwards would have seen him surpass 1,000 receiving yards. Per Pro Football Network , he led the NFL with 4.6 yards of separation per catch, and he also tied for the second-most yards after catch per reception among wide receivers with 7.1. Upon hearing the news that Burden limped away from practice on Saturday, there was naturally concern about the health of one of the Bears’ top young players. However, it appears as though the groin injury will have little to no effect on his availability for the regular season. Given the alternative, that’s not a terrible outcome.

The Ravens defeated the Steelers 28-14. (Kara Durrette/Getty Images) | Getty Images Earlier today, the Chicago Bears signed cornerback Beanie Bishop Jr. while waiving long snapper Luke Elkin. Before getting into the defensive backfield, Elkin’s release means that undrafted free agent Beau Gardner is the last long snapper standing and has presumably won the job. The 26-year-old Bishop is the fourth defensive back the Bears have signed since Friday, joining Xavier Woods, Brandon Hill, and William Wright. They also added safety Marlen Sewell on Tuesday. Bishop (5’9”, 182) was originally a UDFA of the Pittsburgh Steelers in 2024, and he appeared in all 17 games as a rookie with 6 starts, recording 4 interceptions and 45 tackles. The Steelers cut him before the 2025 season, and he signed to the New Orleans Saints’ practice squad for all of last year. Bishop was hit with a three-game suspension this offseason, and the Saints waived him in July. Chicago’s defensive back room has been hit hard with injuries of late, as they are also without Cam Lewis, who was carted off the field yesterday with an apparent ankle injury. Defensive coordinator Dennis Allen said he doesn’t think he’ll be out for long, while adding there is no definite timeline. Lewis was cross-training at a couple of positions, but last week’s injury to safety Coby White necessitated a move to safety. When Lewis left practice yesterday, the Bears moved UDFA Skyler Thomas in with the starters. The Bears’ DB room is also missing safety Elijah Hicks and nickelback Kyler Gordon, who are on the PUP list, cornerback Dallis Flowers was placed on IR, K.C. Eziomume and Gervarrius Owens were waived/injured, corner Terrel Smith has been out, Jaylon Jones missed practice yesterday, and Tyrique Stevenson gutted through an injuiry yesterday after getting tangled up with wideout Luyther Burden III. title: Cash, Stash, or Slash: Jonah Jackson
summary: We only have a few more players in our Cash, Stash, or Slash series. We have been looking at several key veterans and will decide in the next 12 months if they should receive an extension (Cash), if the Bears should cut ties (Slash), or if they should wait and see how things go (Stash). […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - DECEMBER 28: Jonah Jackson #73 of the Chicago Bears stands on the sidelines during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game against the San Francisco 49ers at Levi's Stadium on December 28, 2025 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images We only have a few more players in our Cash, Stash, or Slash series. We have been looking at several key veterans and will decide in the next 12 months if they should receive an extension (Cash), if the Bears should cut ties (Slash), or if they should wait and see how things go (Stash). Today, we pivot back to the offensive line to take a look at guard Jonah Jackson. We’ve already looked at Thuney, where we said he was absolutely a “Cash.” The series started with Darnell Wright, who was not only a “Cash,” but he’s a “Cash” this month. And we also looked at Garrett Bradbury, who we said needs to be a “Slash” after this season. Based on performance, Jonah Jackson is 100% a “Cash” player. But the question is, how many offensive linemen are the Bears comfortable paying on large contracts moving forward? Jonah Jackson: Cash I think before we look at Jackson, let’s look at the Bears’ offensive line construction. I think you see Wright and put his name in ink at tackle at a large salary. I think we look at Thuney and know that he is going to be here at a fairly large salary as long as he wants to be here. But when you look at the other two positions, the Bears will have Logan Jones almost certainly starting at center in 2027, 2028 and 2029 on a rookie salary. I also think it’s almost impossible to think that the Bears LT isn’t going to be on a rookie contract for the next few years. I think the Bears will either be starting Ozzy Trapilo, or they are going to head back to the draft and find a new LT if Trapilo’s knee injury is too much for him to overcome. I think if the Bears have two starting offensive linemen on rookie contracts, there will absolutely be enough cap space for the Bears to pay a third offensive lineman on a veteran contract. Jackson is currently signed through the 2027 season. If Jackson plays as he did in 2025 in 2026, he absolutely needs a contract extension after this season. I’ll be the first to admit that I was a little hesitant on the Jackson trade last year. I know Jackson was solid in Detroit (with Ben Johnson), but his time with the Rams was a mess, and I was concerned that his Rams season was more of what was ahead for Jackson. I was wrong. Jackson not only returned to his Detroit form, but you can argue it was the best season of his career. No, Jackson didn’t receive the accolades, but really great offensive line analysts like Brandon Thorn and Duke Manyweather thought his play last year was as good as any other interior line play in the league. In a recent article for Bleacher Report, Thorn had Jackson ranked as the 10th best guard (both sides combined) in the NFL. Jackson will be 30 heading into the 2027 season, but there’s no reason to think he can’t put together a few more strong seasons in Chicago. As long as his performance in 2026 matches 2025, the Bears should ink Jackson to an extension and help solidify the right side of the offensive line for the next half-decade.

title: Who should be the next Bears player enshrined in the Hall of Fame?
summary: The Chicago Bears still hold the record for the most inductees in the Pro Football Hall of Fame with 41. The Bears also hold the record for the most inductees in the Hall who primarily played their career in the Windy City, with 32. The first ever Bears to get the nod were George Halas, […]
full_text: CHICAGO - DECEMBER 02: Charles Tillman #33 of the Chicago Bears comes down with the ball after an interception in the end zone in front of Plaxico Burress #17 of the New York Giants on December 2, 2007 at Soldier Field in Chicago, Illinois. The Giants defeated the Bears 21-16. (Photo by Jonathan Daniel/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears still hold the record for the most inductees in the Pro Football Hall of Fame with 41. The Bears also hold the record for the most inductees in the Hall who primarily played their career in the Windy City, with 32. The first ever Bears to get the nod were George Halas, Red Grange, and Bronko Nagurski, who were part of the inaugural class in 1963. The most recent primary Bears to be honored were Steve “Mongo” McMichael and Devin Hester, who were in the class of 2024. Julius Peppers (Chicago from 2010 to 2013) was also a part of that class, and class of 2025 inductee Jared Allen played in Chicago in 2014 and 2015. With the Pro Football Hall of Fame officially enshrining its class of 2026 yesterday, I asked our WCG crew which Bears should be next to be inducted. After checking out what we had to say, be sure to share your answer in the comment section. Join the conversation! Sign up for a user account and get: Fewer ads Create community posts Comment on articles, community posts Rec comments, community posts New, improved notifications system! Jeff Berckes: I’m going to focus on the word “should” in the prompt, and to me, that’s easy – Charles Tillman. Peanut changed the game with the Peanut Punch – he even got called out in the Hall of Fame Game broadcast for it, officially kicking off the 2026 NFL season. No one has literally changed the game as much as Peanut’s attacking punch has this century, and no one has had more success with it than he did. Impact plus greatness should be in the HOF despite the media’s slow appreciation of his impact during the early part of his career. Josh Sunderbruch: You could basically just copy Jeff’s argument here for me, because I agree with it entirely. Peanut. Erik Duerrwaechter: It has to be Charles Tillman. Yes, both Jay Hilgenburg and Olin Kreutz are two of the absolute best centers in NFL history. Matt Forte and Lance Briggs impacted the game in their own ways, too. But “Peanut” changed the game forever. His trademarked “Peanut Punch” is a staple for all defensive coaches to teach, and his mindset of attacking the ball with every chance has transformed how we play to this day. Isn’t that the definition of what it means to be in the Hall of Fame? TJ Starman: This is an extremely tough call, and 4 candidates come to mind with 3 as modern candidates and 1 as a senior candidate: Olin Kreutz, Lance Briggs, Charles Tillman, and Jay Hilgenberg (Senior). There are solid cases to be made for each, in my opinion, but my heart is telling me to go with Peanut. His impact on the game far outweighs the accolades of his career (which are far too few in hindsight), and I’d love to see #33 in Canton. Donald Gooch: For me, it is hands down Charles Tillman. I fully endorse the Hall of Fame cases of Hilgenburg, Kreutz, and Briggs. But Tillman not only had a Hall of Fame-worthy career at cornerback for the Bears, but also fundamentally changed the game. We saw the “Peanut Punch” in the Hall of Fame game just this week. Peanut belongs in the Hall, and frankly, it is overdue. Sam Householder: Charles Tillman. There is no question his impact on the game overshadows any “production” or “longevity” knocks among HOF voters (although he had plenty of both of those, too). Lester A. Wiltfong Jr.: Tillman was one of the most underrated players during his time. No one fully appreciated the impact of the Peanut Punch until late in his career, so the individual accolades never came his way. Plus, he was a “zone” cornerback in an era that still gave more publicity to the man-to-man corners, so Pro Bowl voters didn’t know what to do with him. I’d argue his play warrants induction into the Hall, but when you factor in how he changed the game, he should be a slam dunk. And there’s always one, so take us home, MP! Mongo Peanut: I think Olin Kreutz has the best argument. He was a massively underrated part of several successful Bears teams. His leadership, steady hand, and nastiness set an important tone.

title: Joe Burrow is excited to get Erick All Jr. back
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals have largely cycled through tight ends in the Burrow era, finally keeping one for several years with Mike Gesicki after he signed an extension following a successful 2024 season in stripes. However, even with Gesicki playing well, the Bengals have missed having a do-it-all tight end who can go out and catch […]
full_text: The Cincinnati Bengals have largely cycled through tight ends in the Burrow era, finally keeping one for several years with Mike Gesicki after he signed an extension following a successful 2024 season in stripes. However, even with Gesicki playing well, the Bengals have missed having a do-it-all tight end who can go out and catch the ball just as well as he can stay in and block. Based on recent quotes, it seems like Joe Burrow is also excited to get Erick All Jr. back out there on the field. “It’s great to have him back,” Burrow said following a recent practice. “Obviously, he had a lot going on with his knee, but you wouldn’t know it by looking at him. He looks fit, fast, explosive. He’ll play a big role for us this year.” As with the other tight ends on the Bengals roster, Hudson and Gesicki are essentially big receivers who rarely stay in to block, and Sample and Grandy are essentially extra linemen who largely stay in to block and rarely are primary targets on pass plays. A couple of years ago, the Bengals attempted to remedy this by drafting All in the fourth round out of Iowa. Early in the season, it seemed as if he was really transforming the offense, as it was much less predictable what the Bengals would do with him on the field. The new offensive dream died early on in 2024, though, as the reason Erick All fell in the draft struck again and he suffered an injury that not only knocked him out of the rest of 2024, but all of 2025 too. Now, All is back, and if healthy, he can change the Bengals offense into an entirely different beast. The Bengals didn’t put all their eggs in the All basket, however; they drafted Jack Endries in the 2026 NFL Draft, who, like All, may have the potential to play as both a blocker and receiver. The Bengals offense has been great under Burrow even without a do-it-all tight end, but having someone like that can only help the team, so hopefully All can stay healthy this year and going forward.

He has been around the block a few times, so when he says something it does carry a bit of weight. He talked about how this was one of the more physical training camps he has been in, and he called Dexter Lawrence the best defensive lineman in the NFL. Of course, teammates are going to say nice things about each other, but it gives a chance to talk again about having a player like Lawrence could be far more disruptive than someone like Trey Hendrickson at this point in their careers. The most obvious being that Hendrickson is becoming less and less of a three down player, and you can only impact so much when you are just about the only pass rusher on a team. It is also easier to provide help to the edge and for a quarterback to escape. Meanwhile, Lawence will make sure quarterbacks aren’t stepping up in the pocket like they have for years now. He also is going to take up more offensive lineman in the running game, which hopefully will make life easier on the young linebackers to make stops. None of that is diminish the player Hendrickson was with the Bengals, but we are hearing way more about Lawrence in camp (for the right reasons) than we ever did about Hendrickson. Bengals News Quick Hits | Classic Tee Touchdown And Stingy New Defense Highlight Scrimmage Setup “Yes. I’m playing Dexter Lawrence, the best defensive lineman in football,” Karras said. “I get him every day. I wouldn’t call it fun, but it’s a good test of mettle. He always seems to fly under the radar of this high powered offense. He could prove to be a missing piece this offense needs to truly get over the hump. Ja’Marr Chase Sends Clear Warning About Joe Burrow Before NFL Season “I like it when he’s [expletive] pissed,” Chase said. “I’m not gonna lie. I like the fire that he is. He doesn’t always bring it out. He maybe did it once or twice since camp started, but I like it. I like the fire when he has it. “I wanna say his demeanor is just more aggressive. His face is more aggressive, the way he talks is more aggressive, and he got a little mean mug on his face a little bit,” Chase added when asked what “mean” Joe looks like. Some may say the Burrow is looking to prove doubters or outsiders wrong. I think it is more apt to say Burrow is sick of losing. It is part of the reason he threw his weight around to keep Tee Higgins and Ja’Marr Chase. You have really seen him go from a guy who let others be the vocal leaders of the team to a guy who is taking the reigns and trying to will this team to win. Bengals Injury Update: Cincinnati keeping a close eye on two defensive starters, and Shemar Stewart’s expected timeline Soft tissue injuries are quite prevalent in the summer heat of camp. It’s very likely the Bengals are taking it easy with one of their key pieces of the secondary. Not the one that many imagined when he went in the first round to the Minnesota Vikings, but one that many players around the NFL respected. Who’s next for Canton? title: Cashius Howell has been a “monster” in Bengals training camp
summary: If you were caught up in the euphoria of the Bengals trading for Dexter Lawrence and giving up the No. 10 overall pick to acquire him, that maybe overshadowed who the Bengals drafted in the second round this past April. The Bengals selected Texas A&M edge rusher Cashius Howell, their first pick in this year’s […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals defensive end Cashius Howell (55) during minicamp, Tuesday, June 16, 2026, at Kettering Health Practice Fields in downtown Cincinnati. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co If you were caught up in the euphoria of the Bengals trading for Dexter Lawrence and giving up the No. 10 overall pick to acquire him, that maybe overshadowed who the Bengals drafted in the second round this past April. The Bengals selected Texas A&M edge rusher Cashius Howell, their first pick in this year’s draft. Admittedly, I was unimpressed at first. But now, I’m intrigued by what last year’s SEC Defensive Player of the Year can bring to the Bengals’ defensive line. Sports Illustrated’s Albert Breer, one of the most respected writers in the country, recently emptied his Bengals’ notebook and had this to say about the Bengals’ second-round pick. Rookie Cashius Howell would’ve been in a clump of players the Bengals discussed if they hadn’t traded the No. 10 pick, so getting the Texas A&M rusher in the second round was seen internally as a coup. He’s been a monster in camp thus far, bringing the speed and explosiveness he flashed in college, and more strength than some expected. Howell made waves when he put Orlando Brown Jr. on his back this past week. That’s not just any offensive lineman, either. Brown is 6’8” and 350 pounds. The fact that Howell did that to him says a lot about his strength and where he is headed into his rookie season. The Bengals may need Howell to step up early with Shemar Stewart being out for several weeks with a hyperextended knee. Playing alongside Boye Mafe and Myles Murphy gives Howell veterans to learn from, which is great. But Howell isn’t just another edge rusher from Texas A&M the Bengals drafted. He can play, and he can be a difference-maker off the edge. Much of the attention is on Stewart, Mafe, and Murphy, but do not overlook Howell.

title: Al Golden likes what he’s seeing from Jordan Battle as he enters a pivotal season
summary: While Bryan Cook has been given a lot of credit and attention for the outstanding training camp he’s been having, don’t forget about Jordan Battle. Through his first three seasons, he’s had his ups and downs. But you can see the hustle and the playmaking abilities, as evidenced by his four interceptions in 2025. In […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - NOVEMBER 27: Jordan Battle #27 of the Cincinnati Bengals warms up prior to an NFL football game against the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium on November 27, 2025 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images While Bryan Cook has been given a lot of credit and attention for the outstanding training camp he’s been having, don’t forget about Jordan Battle. Through his first three seasons, he’s had his ups and downs. But you can see the hustle and the playmaking abilities, as evidenced by his four interceptions in 2025. In addition, there was the hustle play to punch the ball out of Baltimore Ravens tight end Isiah Likely’s possession on Thanksgiving Night in Baltimore, just as he was about to score a touchdown after catching a long pass from Lamar Jackson. “Jordan’s having a great camp,” defensive coordinator Al Golden told Dan Hoard . “I love where he’s at mentally. He’s prepared and he’s in great condition.” Hoard, who posts his five observations from every training camp practice on his Twitter account, said Battle forced a fumble against running back Chase Brown during Friday night’s practice. Although Brown recovered the ball, it’s still another positive development for Battle entering a contract year. Battle has never been the problem in the Bengals’ secondary. He has a great mindset, and he has always had one. But look at the safeties he has played alongside in the first three seasons of his career. Nick Scott, who was serviceable but not a game-changer. Geno Stone, please. And then there’s Vonn Bell, who was not the same in his second stint with the Bengals as he was in his first stint when he played a key role in the team going to the Super Bowl. Now, Battle gets to play with Bryan Cook. Yes, Cook has only played one more season in the NFL than Battle. But he’s a former second-round pick, two-time Super Bowl champion, and entering his prime. That matters, and it also matters that Cook can bring leadership he learned playing in Steve Spagnuolo’s defense for four years. Battle is in a much better position to take another step this season and become a more well-rounded player, and it’s great to see him performing at a high level throughout training camp. full_text: Cincinnati Bengals safety Jordan Battle (27) chats with young fans during practice at the Paycor Stadium practice facility in downtown Cincinnati on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Cincinnati Bengals have officially reached the point of training camp where the pads are on, the competition is intensifying, and some of the biggest storylines are beginning to separate themselves from the usual camp noise. Through the first seven practices, perhaps the biggest development has been the way the Bengals’ revamped defense has consistently challenged Joe Burrow and an offense that entered camp with sky-high expectations. And, unsurprisingly, Dexter Lawrence has been at the center of it all. The massive defensive tackle has quickly established himself as a disruptive force, routinely creating problems for the offensive line and forcing the Bengals to speed up their operation. Joe Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase and Ted Karras have all taken notice of what Lawrence is bringing to practice, with Karras even calling him one of the best nose tackles he’s faced in his career. Lawrence hasn’t been the only defensive player making noise, either. Bryan Cook has continued to stand out in the secondary, while players such as Barrett Carter, Demetrius Knight Jr. and others have benefited from the attention Lawrence commands up front. The Bengals’ defense has looked faster, more physical and more confident than it did for much of last season, giving Zac Taylor and defensive coordinator Al Golden plenty to be encouraged about as camp moves forward. On the other side of the ball, the offense has still produced plenty of its own highlights. Burrow continues to show the chemistry that makes Cincinnati’s passing attack so dangerous, particularly with Chase and Tee Higgins, while Chase Brown is making his case for a prominent role in the offense during what could be a pivotal season for him. The Bengals have also experimented with more 13-personnel looks, adding another wrinkle to an offense that could look somewhat different in 2026. That brings us to Day 8, which should provide another opportunity to see whether the defense can maintain its early momentum or whether Burrow and company begin to push back. The Bengals are now deep enough into camp that individual matchups are becoming increasingly meaningful, particularly along the offensive and defensive lines. title: Browns: D-line looking to be ‘sudden, violent and fast’
summary: The Cleveland Browns have completed the first two weeks of training camp, with only about 99 percent of the focus being on the depressing battle to see who will be the starting quarterback. Fortunately, other areas of the team will play a role in determining how well the 2026 season goes, starting with the defensive […]
full_text: Jared Verse #8 and Mason Graham #94 (Photo by Nick Cammett/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cleveland Browns have completed the first two weeks of training camp, with only about 99 percent of the focus being on the depressing battle to see who will be the starting quarterback. Fortunately, other areas of the team will play a role in determining how well the 2026 season goes, starting with the defensive line. The biggest change, of course, is that defensive end Myles Garrett is out and Jared Verse is in his place. Following at a very close second is Mike Rutenberg taking over as defensive coordinator for the departed Jim Schwartz. While Rutenberg is bringing some fresh ideas to the defense , many of his core philosophies are similar to what Schwartz likes to do, and there is the added benefit that six of the defensive coaches are holdovers from last year, which brings a nice sense of familiarity and comfort to the defense. One of those coaches is Jacques Cesaire, who is tasked with getting the most out of a defensive line that no longer features the game’s best defensive player. But that doesn’t take away from what Cesaire wants to see from the defensive line, as he explained during his media session on Saturday ( quotes via a team-provided transcript ): “The engine of the defense simply means this: we’ve made a deal with the entire organization that when the ball is thrown, we’re going to sprint to the ball. We’re going to be first on the scene to deliver the blow on whoever catches the ball or is trying to run the ball. That’s the first part of the engine. “The second part of the engine is we get to establish the violence. We’re the first line of defense, so we get to establish the violence, the mentality of the entire defense. So, those guys take a lot of pride in it. We talk about it every single day, we preach it every single day, we practice it every single day. We take pride in the fact that the defense is trusting us with that title. “I just want them to play sudden, violent, and fast.” #Browns DT Mason Graham and DE Logan Fano going head-to-head in a get-off drill competition. pic.twitter.com/JGSn5U8LhM — Camryn Justice (@camijustice) August 3, 2026 Verse has claimed a considerable amount of attention since arriving in town, while second-year defensive tackle Mason Graham has quietly gone about his business. Now that he has a year under his belt, Cesaire is expecting even more from one of the defense’s smartest players: “He just understands football, understands formations and what the offense is trying to do, and he’s trying to help everybody out as much as he can, and he gets down, and he starts rolling. It’s been really cool to see that maturation out of him. This is a guy who knows exactly what’s going on, and he’s letting everybody know. It’s like having a second Mike linebacker out there. It’s really good for us.” Cleveland has been dealing with injuries at defensive tackle throughout training camp, as Maliek Collins is on the PUP list, Graham and Mike Hall Jr. have missed practice time with minor injuries, and Sam Kamara and Kalia Davis are dealing with injuries. That has provided an opportunity for some lesser-known players like Travis Bell, Elijah Chatman, and Tyreek Sapp to show what they can do, which has Cesaire excited for the first preseason game against the Chicago Bears: “Tyreek Sapp is a name that comes up. He’s grown so fast, from where he started to where he is now; I’m extremely proud of him. Adin (Huntington) has been Adin, as usual. Just a ball of energy, a Swiss Army knife who can play inside or outside; he has enough speed to do both. And you guys are going to love “Snacks”. T-Bell (Travis Bell), we just got him, and he just works. I’m really excited to see what these guys do next Saturday. We’re tuning them up right now for all of that. I just can’t wait; I am excited football is back.” It might take some time to get used to seeing Cleveland’s defense without Garrett and Schwartz, but if the defensive line can be the sudden, violent and fast unit that Cesaire wants them to be, then the difference may be negligible. And they may even help to take some of the focus off the ongoing mess at quarterback.
