title: David Walker turning heads at camp
summary: It’s easy to find hopium through training camp practices and reports. That can be dangerous, but at least it can also offer clues on who to pay closer attention to as joint team practices and preseason games draw closer. In a do-or-die year for Todd Bowles’s defense, there have been some early bright spots that […]
full_text: TAMPA, FL - JULY 31: Tampa Bay Buccaneers Linebacker David Walker (51) goes thru drills during Training Camp on July 31, 2026 at the AdventHealth Training Center at One Buccaneer Place in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Cliff Welch/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images It’s easy to find hopium through training camp practices and reports. That can be dangerous, but at least it can also offer clues on who to pay closer attention to as joint team practices and preseason games draw closer. In a do-or-die year for Todd Bowles’s defense, there have been some early bright spots that should be stoking some excitement. Namely, pass rusher David Walker, who tore his ACL during last training camp, seems to have rebounded in a big way. If reports are to be believed, Walker has been consistently disruptive, logging a would-be sack in eight straight practices so far. Bucs edge David Walker gets a rep on Luke Goedeke here. pic.twitter.com/wdSCm0aRPA — Logan B. Robinson (@LogansTwitty) August 3, 2026 The 2025 4th round pick received plenty of hype last year too, prior to his injury. Walker, who was one of the most dominant pass rushers in FCS history, carries an unorthodox, sawed-off frame (just under 6-1, 263 pounds) but pairs it with excellent power and bend. His physical limitations and subpar competition made him a Day 3 pick, but the potential has always existed. Smartly not counting on a recovering Walker being a primary solution to the ailing pass rush, the Buccaneers already invested heavily in the position this off-season. They signed Al-Quadin Muhammad in free agency and drafted prolific Miami edge rusher Reuben Bain Jr. in the first round to team with stalwart Yaya Diaby, who’s entering a contract year. GM Jason Licht went so far as to say this week that excitement for Walker has been on an “even plane” with Bain, and Bain has been impressive in his own right so that’s really saying something. With the re-stocked edge rushing corps getting the added benefit of Walker looking fully recuperated, the Bucs might just be able to turn their pass-rushing luck around. Tampa has failed to see any player record double-digit sacks in nearly five years, when Shaq Barrett notched 10 in 2021. More often than not, it’s defensive tackles who have been leading the charge on the sack front (namely Vita Vea), and while interior pressure is important, no threats on the edge will too often leave the opposing QB unpressured and the coverage unit out to dry. If Walker can maintain his torrid start, he’d be an invaluable rotational rusher to relieve Diaby and Bain, as well as mixing and matching with them and Muhammad to create diverse pressure packages. With the first game against the New York Jets coming August 14, eyes will be on Walker to see if there’s indeed something to be excited about.

Replacing a player of that caliber is a tall task, especially this late in the offseason. Washington may add to its offensive line — for depth, if not more — but for now, the plan is to turn to Brandon Coleman at left tackle, according to a team source who spoke on condition of anonymity because they are not authorized to speak publicly on the matter. Coleman, a former third-round pick out of TCU, is capable of playing all five spots on the line and started at left tackle for most of the 2024 season, when Washington reached the NFC Championship Game after going 12-5 in the regular season. Coleman spent much of this offseason training with Tunsil at University of Alabama, where he was immersed in Tunsil’s intense pre-camp regimen and worked with Tunsil’s personal strength and conditioning coach, nutritionist, chef and offensive line specialist. Moving Coleman back to left tackle allows Washington to keep Paul at left guard and Josh Conerly Jr. at right tackle, where he started last season as a rookie after playing on the left side at University of Oregon. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE From Last Man Standig: Nobody expects Coleman to perform at Tunsil’s high-end level, but there are reasons to think he can be effective on the outside. Having a replacement with Coleman’s upside is a relative luxury in an era where every team desperately searches for quality starting linemen. Having Coleman and Paul start would thin out the offensive line depth. Swing tackle Andrew Wylie is the likely primary backup at both tackle spots, though his playing experience is largely on the right side. For more from Ben Standig, click here From Sports Illustrated: The ripples of Laremy Tunsil’s injury will be felt until he returns, but the team is at least positioned to reshuffle what they already have. Now, we all will be waiting to see Coleman take the first-team left tackle reps when Washington returns to practice and what the corresponding first-team alignment looks like at left guard. Coleman has made 20 starts across the regular season and playoffs, with 18 of them coming at left tackle. According to Pro Football Focus, he played 390 total snaps in 2025, allowed 11 pressures and only one QB hit, gave up zero sacks, and earned a 64.6 overall grade . He basically revamped my whole approach to how I treat camp and the season. There’s a lot of stuff that I took from him, from his nutritionist to his strength guy, working with a chef, just taking care of my body a lot better. My prep for practice is a lot different. Seeing how a guy like that prepares, how he treats his body, what he does in his off time and how he recovers — that’s the type of stuff that you can’t get anywhere. There’s only one Laremy Tunsil, in my opinion. The best tackle in the league. There’s no way to gloss this over. But football is a team game and the Eagles won’t care who lines up at left tackle come September 13th. Keep this in mind too: David Blough ’s offense will look much different than Kliff Kingsbury ’s scheme did. Daniels will not line up in the shotgun on nearly every snap. There will be more misdirection, there will be more play action, and there will likely be a better run game. All of those things will help the offensive line, with or without Tunsil. And don’t forget the Commanders did just sign Stef Diggs. It’s not good news. Losing Tunsil is bad news. But the season ain’t over yet either. It hasn’t even begun. Coleman allowed 11 pressures, only 1 QB hit and zero sacks, according to @PFF . pic.twitter.com/NIIWjRL8JG — Scott Abraham (@Scott7news) August 9, 2026 To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Hogs Haven Just How Much Does Diggs Move the Needle for WAS? How much does Diggs move the needle for the WAS receiving corps? A ton. Compared to the 20 teams to have played in the last 10 Super Bowls, and before the signing of Diggs, you could make a credible case for the top 3 WAS receivers to be a SB-caliber group only if you included Chig Okonkwo as #2 and Rachaad White as #3. You could not argue that the WR group alone was SB-caliber. Terry is a solid #1, but anyone else would have to had a breakthrough year for the WR corp to have been credible – something tough to count on. Now, there is no question that the wide receivers and the receivers overall are SB caliber. You can count on both McLaurin and Diggs to get 80 catches and over 1000 yards receiving. McLaurin had 82 catches for 1096 yards in 2024, his last healthy year. His career averages (mostly with bad QBs) are 79 for 1106 yards. Diggs had 85 catches for 1013 yards last year, despite returning from ACL surgery midway through the prior year. His career averages are 99 catches for 1215 yards. I’d say 80 catches for 1000 yards from both of them is so safe a bet that it might be illegal. Chig is about average for a receiver #3 at any position. That means that without having a breakthrough year, but rather just repeating what they’ve already accomplished, Washington’s receiving corp is already Super Bowl caliber. title: The Cold, Hard Truth – Life more difficult for Commanders without Laremy Tunsil
summary: I often get accused of pumping out too many rainbows and unicorns when it comes to our favorite team in Washington. Well, this post will not have any mythical creatures or pots of gold at the end. Yesterday’s loss of left tackle Laremy Tunsil to a torn triceps is DEVASTATING for this football team! There […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MD - SEPTEMBER 21: Laremy Tunsil #78 of the Washington Commanders walks off of the field at halftime during an NFL football game against the Las Vegas Raiders at Northwest Stadium on September 21, 2025 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images I often get accused of pumping out too many rainbows and unicorns when it comes to our favorite team in Washington. Well, this post will not have any mythical creatures or pots of gold at the end. Yesterday’s loss of left tackle Laremy Tunsil to a torn triceps is DEVASTATING for this football team! There is no other way to put this. Losing Laremy Tunsil for ANY amount of time SUCKS! Tunsil is the best player on the team , a top three left tackle in the league and a veteran presence that was desperately needed along this offensive line. Although this team now has some really deep REDS (far more than we’ve had in the past decade), Laremy was the Commanders only BLUE. I will not sit here and play doctor and try to guestimate just how long it will take him to return but based on all reports I’m seeing regarding his type of injury, it will be months. How does Tunsil’s loss affect play-calling? This is a tough one… The last two seasons under offensive coordinator Kliff Kingsbury, Washington was a shotgun team. This season under David Blough, the Commanders are expected to be under center quite a bit, with a heavy focus on the run game. Tunsil is a good (not great) run blocker, and the team should be able to get by in a scheme that utilizes a lot of outside zone running. Where his loss will be felt most is in the passing game. Laremy is one of the best pass-protecting tackles in the league. He has elite footwork, strong hands and anchors well. The concern with being under center and running play-action, is that Jayden Daniels will be turning his back to the defense and these play-action shots do take a bit more time to develop. Whoever steps in at left tackle will need to make sure they are capable of protecting his blindside and allowing our receivers to work downfield. In normal dropbacks, I would expect to see Blough keep a tight end in more often to help or have a running back chip. Of course, keeping a tight end in to block will eliminate them from being a threat in the passing game, but keeping Jayden upright is the bigger concern. Creative play-calling, something Blough’s offense is supposed to hinge on, can also help whoever steps in. Motions and shifts can be utilized to put guys in the best spots to succeed, be that receivers or tight ends getting open quickly, or players being moved to help that left side. Who can step up? The logical choice of players who are currently on the roster is third-year lineman Brandon Coleman. As of now, I’m told the plan is to move Brandon Coleman back to left tackle, where he was the starter in 2024. https://t.co/HkBMKppsf7 — Nicki Jhabvala (@NickiJhabvala) August 9, 2026 Coleman is no stranger to left tackle. He started 22 games at TCU on the left side and as a rookie with Washington, he had 12 starts at left tackle during the regular season and started all three playoff games. He’s a solid run blocker so this outside zone system should fit him well, and when he gets his hands firing in conjunction with his feet, he can do a good job in pass protection. The area he needs to improve is consistency with his hand placement and not over-setting which allows defenders to cross his face and get inside. Way too many times as a rookie he was beaten on outside moves where his feet were ok, but his hands were not. The oversetting can be corrected and solid play from Chris Paul to his right may also help here, but don’t kid yourself, he’s nowhere near the player Tunsil is, and pretending he is will only bring disappointment. Daniels to Noah Brown at the goal line – but LOOK at the block by the rookie Brandon Coleman here 💪🏻💪🏻💪🏻 pic.twitter.com/MDjuHb2f5i — Tiller56 (Hogs Haven) (@Tiller56) September 24, 2024 #Commanders Brandon Coleman played 242 snaps at left tackle last year, allowing 0 sacks, 0 QB hits, and 5 pressures (2.1% pressure rate) The pressure rate allowed was even better than Laremy Tunsil's elite 3.1%, with the obvious caveat that the gameplan changed when he filled in… — Full Command (@FullCommandShow) August 9, 2026 There is also a chance that Adam Peters puts in a call to unrestricted free agent tackle Taylor Decker. At 32, Decker still offers good ability and he’s a guy who has played for Ben Johnson, so his learning curve in the new offense may not be that steep. My understanding is that Brandon Coleman is the LT for the season. I haven’t heard anything about adding another player, but I would personally call Taylor Decker immediately. Has a relationship with Blough, and KNOWS the offense already. No brainer. #Commanders pic.twitter.com/XcnQtk9zdN — Josh Taylor (@JoshTaylorFB) August 9, 2026 Any way you slice it, this is a HUGE blow to an offense that was just seeming to click. The recent addition of Stefon Diggs gave hope to many Commanders fans that we had the firepower to compete for the NFC title. This recent setback dampens that hope a bit – as losing your best player often does. Let’s all hope Brandon Coleman is ready to step up to the challenge, or we can lure Taylor Decker to Washington to step in while Tunsil recovers. As is the case in football, the next-man-up mentality will truly be tested in Washington. If there is any silver lining to Tunsil’s injury, it’s that it happened early in training camp – which now give the Commanders time to prepare for the regular season. May the force be with us!

Rebilas-Imagn Images | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con The Washington Commanders got some unfortunate injury news on Saturday night. Left tackle Laremy Tunsil left the field after a 1-on-1 with Odafe Oweh, and was taken to the team facility for evaluation. An MRI showed he tore his triceps , which will likely require surgery. He is expected to miss most, of not all, of his second season with the Commanders. Tunsil just signed a 2-year, $60 million contract extension that reestablish him as the highest-paid LT in the league. The big question everyone wanted answered yesterday was who would replace Tunsil at LT . Andrew Wylie replaced him in practice Saturday, but he has only played five snaps there in his career. Brandon Coleman was Washington’s starting left tackle during his rookie season in 2024 and he filled in for Tunsil for the last three games of the 2025 season. The Athletic ‘s Nicki Jhabvala reports that the plan is for Coleman to move back to his former position of left tackle. He had been in a training camp battle with Chris Paul for the starting left guard position. Coleman started last season at left guard, before ceding the starting role to Paul for the remainder of the games. Coleman has started 18 games at left tackle for the Commanders, and will now enter his third season getting time at the position. There was speculation that GM Adam Peters could bring in a free agent like Taylor Decker, or move second-year OT Josh Conerly Jr. to his college position on the left side. Washington could still bring in a veteran for competition, but for now, Coleman has the job. title: Wednesday’s joint practice is more critical than the 1st preseason game
summary: In this week’s Reacts survey, we asked what Hogs Haven readers were interested in with respect to the scheduled joint practice at Ashburn and preseason game in Landover vs the visiting Miami Dolphins next week. The results underscore the relative sophistication of the survey respondents and reflect recent NFL trends in training camp and preseason […]
full_text: Miami Dolphins' running back #31 Ollie Gordon II (2R) is tackled during the NFL match between Miami Dolphins and Washington Commanders at Santiago Bernabeu Stadium in Madrid on November 16, 2025. (Photo by Oscar DEL POZO / AFP) (Photo by OSCAR DEL POZO/AFP via Getty Images) | AFP via Getty Images In this week’s Reacts survey , we asked what Hogs Haven readers were interested in with respect to the scheduled joint practice at Ashburn and preseason game in Landover vs the visiting Miami Dolphins next week. The results underscore the relative sophistication of the survey respondents and reflect recent NFL trends in training camp and preseason preparation. Visit our partners at FanDuel These poll results are indicative of a greater truth: the traditional NFL preseason game is dying. In its place, a more efficient, high-stakes alternative has taken over the month of August: the joint practice. For decades, NFL training camps were isolated grinds. Teams stayed on their own campuses, hitting the same teammates for three weeks before playing highly scripted preseason games where starters barely saw the field. Today, the landscape is completely different. Joint practices, where two franchises meet at a training facility for a few days of controlled, intensely competitive scrimmages, have become the focal point of the summer. The numbers trace a clear shift in league philosophy. In 2014, roughly one-third of the league participated in joint sessions. By 2019, that number had climbed to more than 20 teams. In the wake of the 2020 pandemic disruptions, the trend accelerated rapidly. When the NFL officially reduced the preseason from 4 games to 3 in 2021, joint practices shifted from a useful option to a near-absolute necessity. By 2024, a record 28 of the 32 NFL teams scheduled at least one joint practice, with several teams booking multiple sessions across the month. The primary driver of this growth is control. In a standard preseason game, a head coach cannot control the environment. They cannot, for example, risk their starting quarterback taking a blindside hit from an opposing defensive end who is on the roster bubble and trying to make an impression on his coaches. Joint practices do a lot to solve this issue. Coaches are able to agree ahead of time on specific rules such as no tackling of the quarterback, quick whistles on run plays, and specific situational drills like third-and-long or two-minute drills. This environment allows starters to get high-quality, game-speed repetitions without the standard game risks. A starting offense can run 40 plays against a premier first-string defense from the opposite conference—something that never happens in modern preseason games where starters sit on the bench to avoid injury. Coaches get film of their top players executing the actual playbook against unfamiliar schemes and elite talent. Dan Quinn discussed some of the benefits of joint practice during his press conference prior to Saturday’s practice: One, I like it for the competitiveness. You know, going against the same guys, you starting to learn formations and players and people. So, [I] like [joint practice] for the sake of [going] against I new group. I also like it for the evaluation of that too — of seeing who steps up. And then, in the practice itself, it might be a little bit more creative than the actual games, meaning…where you may not show some of those in the games, but in the practice you may work [on them] a little bit more. I like that we get skill work, one-on- ones, and then, in the team period, some scripted, some not. [Also, is the evaluation versus another team]; are we behind in an area? Is this an area that needs more attention? Or, this is taking longer than we [want] to get ready. Dan Quinn talked about the importance of joint practices. The Washington Commanders will be sharing the field with the Miami Dolphins on Wednesday. pic.twitter.com/HhxEJr0Dqq — COMMANDERS FOOTBALL (@HogsHaven) August 8, 2026 Fans have noticed this shift in quality, causing a surge in interest that is reflected in our Reacts survey results this week. Public attendance at these sessions has skyrocketed. Fans realize that if they buy a ticket to a mid-August preseason game, they will spend three hours watching third-string players who may not make the final 53-man roster. Conversely, attending a joint practice guarantees a great seat to see elite matchups, like an All-Pro wide receiver going head-to-head against a lockdown cornerback in one-on-one drills. The media coverage reflects this fan demand. Local radio stations now broadcast live from the sidelines; national insiders track daily wins and losses, and social media clips of practice touchdowns generate millions of views. For the modern fan, joint practices offer raw, unfiltered access to the highest level of football competition weeks before the regular season begins. On Saturday , DQ addressed whether joint practices are more critical to creating controlled competition for starters than preseason games: I think there’s probably some balance where it’s not just one or the other, but having two of them [joint practice & preseason game] certainly helps. And so, for us, [facing] Miami [and] Baltimore with a game sandwiched in between, I like how that flows. But as far as who plays what and how much, I think that’s a good ‘next week question’. But what I can say is that there’s a lot of value in these [joint practices] and I can see, moving forward, why they’re good for the league, [and] good for us — not as an alternative to a game, but [as an] addition to it. pic.twitter.com/eDPYgxJxEW — COMMANDERS FOOTBALL (@HogsHaven) August 8, 2026 The model, of course, is not without issues. The most prominent risk of joint practices is the inevitable outbreak of fights. When two groups of highly competitive athletes compete in the summer heat after weeks of practicing against their own teammates, tempers flare. Most Commanders fans above the age of 20 will probably remember that, during a 2015 joint training camp session in Richmond, Virginia, tension boiled over between Jay Gruden’s Washington squad and Bill O’Brien’s Houston Texans. A series of skirmishes escalated into a massive, multi-field brawl involving large groups of players from both teams. Unable to restore order and fearing potential injuries, Gruden and O’Brien chose to completely separate the teams and finish the day on isolated fields. Following the incident, which was featured prominently on HBO’s Hard Knocks, Gruden lamented the wasted opportunity for productive work. Furthermore, the risk of injury is never completely zero. Even without live tackling, players still suffer non-contact tears or collisions at full speed. When a star player goes down during a joint session, critics quickly question the wisdom of putting players in such a high-intensity environment before September. Washington fans were reminded, this week, of the fact that practices are not without risk. On Saturday, starting left tackle Laremy Tunsil suffered a torn tricep in a one-on-one drill versus Odafe Oweh. However, it seems that the benefits continue to outweigh the drawbacks for NFL front offices. The controlled environment protects players better than live game action, while still providing the evaluation data that general managers need to cut the roster down to 53 players. As long as the 3-game preseason model remains (or when the 2-game model is inevitably introduced along with the 18-game season), the joint practice will continue to rise in importance as a centerpiece of the NFL summer. Joint practice The Commanders joint practice with the Dolphins is scheduled to take place on Wednesday, August 12th. It will get extensive coverage by local media, and Hogs Haven will provide the usual updates throughout the day. First preseason game Washington’s first preseason game is less than two weeks away; it will be a home game vs the Miami Dolphins on Friday, August 14th at 7:00 p.m.…

summary: The Daily Slop – 9 August 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - SEPTEMBER 28: Laremy Tunsil #78 of the Washington Commanders stands on the sideline during the second half of an NFL 2025 game against the Atlanta Falcons at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on September 28, 2025 in Atlanta, Georgia. Enjoy! Commanders links Laremy Tunsil signed a $30M per year contract in the offseason and was tasked with protecting Jayden Daniels’ blindside. Now, out most if not all of the regular season. https://t.co/v7jCaCS25t — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) August 9, 2026 Fan video from Washington Commanders training camp today of Laremy Tunsil suffering a torn triceps in a drill vs Odafe Oweh. pic.twitter.com/lTIp0O4NF1 — COMMANDERS FOOTBALL (@HogsHaven) August 9, 2026 Brandon Coleman, you’re up got damnit. — Jamual (@LetMualTellit) August 9, 2026 At Oregon, Josh Conerly Jr. started 28 games at left tackle. Protect Jayden’s blindside. — Scott Abraham (@Scott7news) August 9, 2026 Wouldn’t be shocked if Adam Peters is already on the phone with Taylor Decker & his reps. The team still values Brandon Coleman’s versatility (went to an NFC title game with him at LT in ‘24) but hard to believe Washington is ok with Andrew Wylie potentially protecting Jayden… — Ryan Fowler (@_RyanFowler_) August 9, 2026 Articles ESPN Commanders LT Laremy Tunsil suffers torn triceps It’s a crucial blow to the Commanders’ offense, costing the team a player considered one of the best at his position. The recovery time for such an injury is typically at least four months and as long as six or seven. The Commanders have veteran tackle Andrew Wylie, but the bulk of his career has been spent on the right side. He has played five snaps at left tackle since entering the league in 2017. He typically replaced Tunsil when he would miss a practice. But Washington also has Coleman, who started 12 games at left tackle as a rookie in 2024 and three more last year when Tunsil was injured. Coleman has been competing with Chris Paul at left guard. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE From Last Man Standig: Third-year lineman Brandon Coleman, part of Washington’s left guard competition, is the logical replacement. The 2024 third-round pick started 12 games at left tackle in 2024 and filled in last season when an injured Tunsil sat out the final three weeks. Second-year right tackle Josh Conerly Jr., Washington’s 2025 first-round pick, played left tackle at Oregon. Moving him to the left side would create two changes, but a potential option. Andrew Wylie, a starter at tackle and guard during his nine-year career, is Washington’s primary backup tackle, but his playing experience comes mainly from the right side. Neither Wylie nor reserve Trent Scott is a long-term answer at left tackle. For more from Ben Standig, click here From The Athletic (paywall) : Washington will have reshuffle its front five and potentially look for outside help for depth, if not more. Andrew Wylie has been the team’s primary backup left tackle throughout camp and took over for Tunsil for the remainder of Saturday’s practice. But he’s not the only in-house option the team may turn to. The Commanders could also ask second-year tackle Josh Conerly Jr., who played primarily on the left side in college, to shift back there from the right side. It may also look to Brandon Coleman, the third-year lineman who is versatile enough to play all five spots up front. Coleman has been competing for the starting left guard spot in camp, but he was the team’s primary starting left tackle in 2024. Quinn declined, however, to move Coleman earlier in camp when starting center Nick Allegretti went down with a calf injury, opting instead to use Julian Good-Jones and let Coleman focus on left guard. Allegretti has attended recent camp practices but has not participated. That he wasn’t placed on the physically unable to perform list indicates the team does not expect the calf to be a long-term issue, but it has not provided a clear timetable for his expected return. In his absence, Washington has signed four linemen — centers Trey Hill and Daniel Brunskill, guard Max Scharping and tackle Nicholas Petit-Frere — for depth and competition. Washington’s injury problems run even deeper. Shortly after Tunsil went down, cornerback Trey Amos left practice with an unknown injury. He had been activated from PUP only a day earlier after a lengthy recovery from a fractured fibula. To read more of this article from The Athletic, CLICK HERE Sports Illustrated Nicholas Petit-Frere Arrived at an Interesting Time The team had unbelievable timing by signing Petit-Frere several hours before Tunsil went down with the injury. Petit-Frere has 28 starts across 34 games, but has played primarily at right tackle. Petit-Frere has left-side experience from his time at Ohio State, where he started 12 games at left tackle in 2021. While Petit-Frere may have been an option if he had been around all of camp, since he has not, he will find himself a week behind in a complicated setup. Washington Does Not Have to Choose Just One Solution One solution is to not pick one solution. Washington could choose to move multiple pieces rather than simply replacing Tunsil with one backup. Wylie, Coleman, and Conerly are all prime examples of versatile linemen who can move around at different spots. Then, of course, there is always the possibility that none of these players are what they are looking for, and Adam Peters could still look outside , beyond the doors at Ashburn. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Bullock’s Film Room (subscription) From September 2024 : Brandon Colman shows promise against Bengals Coleman had some struggles last week against the Giants, who have two excellent edge rushers in Kayvon Thibodeaux and Brian Burns. This week, he faced off against Bengals pass rusher Trey Hendrickson, who is coming off a career year last season with 17.5 sacks. My biggest concern with Coleman after the draft was his tendency to rely on two-handed punches . Coleman is strong and when he lands those two-handed punches, they have a big impact. He can really stun defenders and knock them off their initial rush plan, which makes it an effective move. However, in the NFL, shooting both hands at the same time can cause issues. Coleman tends to throw both hands without following up with his feet, resulting in him lunging at rushers. Here we see a good example of Coleman lunging slightly at Hendrickson. He feels Hendrickson approaching and looks to land his strong two-handed punch, firing both hands at the same time. On this occasion, he manages to land both hands, which stuns Hendrickson’s rush. However, you can also see the traits that lead this to be a worrying technique. If you pause the clip as Coleman lands his punch, you can see his arms are fully extended, his shoulders and head are leaning forward and his center of gravity is pulled forward from under his feet to out in front of his feet. You can get away with that occasionally in the NFL and a lot more frequently in college, but use that type of technique consistently against the best rushers in the league and they will take advantage. Fortunately, Coleman has clearly been working on this issue throughout the offseason and only used his two-handed punch on rare occasions in this game. Instead, he leaned much more heavily on a different technique known as hand flashing. This time we see a good example of a hand flash technique. As Coleman slides out towards Hendrickson, he extends his outside arm out towards the rusher. This is very normal and Hendrickson assumes that Coleman is just looking to get his hand on him to try and cut off the rush to the edge, so he responds accordingly.…

title: 2026 Arizona Cardinals training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Follow our daily updates from Cardinals training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The Arizona Cardinals ' camp is at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Arizona, and Cardinals reporter Josh Weinfuss has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and, of course, the quarterback room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Cardinals camp. We will update this file often. How will Arizona's quarterback situation shake out with  Jacoby Brissett  back on a reworked contract? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive into all the updates and check back for more information until the first full week of the preseason begins Thursday.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest on the Cardinals 
 
 Tyler Allgeier 'building' relationship with rookie RB Jeremiyah Love 
 Source: Cardinals' Brissett guaranteed $15.5M in reworked deal 
 Cardinals TE Trey McBride walks back dig at Arizona fanbase 
 Sweat (knee) among four Cards added to PUP list 
 With deal done, Brissett can focus on Cardinals' playbook 
 

 

 Aug. 9 

 Cardinals starting quarterback Jacoby Brissett struggled with the deep ball throughout practice Sunday, missing approximately seven deep balls. Some were long. Some were wide. Four were to Marvin Harrison Jr .

 It was an atypical performance from Brissett, who, until Sunday, had been consistent with his deep balls throughout training camp, typically putting them in a place where only his receivers can catch them.

 After practice, Brissett set out to rectify his misses.

 He and Harrison spent about 15 minutes working on deep balls from approximately 30 yards. It looked as though Brissett was working on his deep touch to get his passes where Harrison can make a play.

 
 Rookie quarterback Carson Beck had a strong finish to Sunday's practice. He hit rookie wide receiver  Reggie Virgil  for a touchdown in the back of the end zone and had a quiet celebration to himself afterward. That came after Beck hit wide receiver Bryson Green on a deep ball but then threw an interception. 
 The Cardinals tried a variety of defensive lineups Sunday. At one point, third-year cornerback Elijah Jones , who has played defense in just one game in his career, took first-team snaps. Second-year defensive back Kitan Crawford , who played 12 games on defense last season, also got some first-team reps. 
 Wide receiver Ihmir Smith-Marsette continued his impressive camp with another touchdown Sunday. He continues to make big catches and has been consistently making plays throughout camp. 
 

 

 Aug. 4 
 Thursday night's Hall of Fame game will not just be a run-through for the players, it will also be the first time the Cardinals' coaching staff will have a chance to be together during a game.

 "I think that's another great thing for us to have this game, to just get a little quick dry run-through on how game day operations go, just from time management, all that stuff," offensive coordinator Nathaniel Hackett said. "I think it's going to be great for all of us and there'll be some ups and downs and you work through those and grow every day."

 Hackett said he'll be in the booth watching the action unfold from above but with new coach Mike LaFleur calling the plays and quarterback coach Matt Schaub handling Carson Beck , Hackett will be able to help whoever needs help. But that'll also be part of this staff's first time together: Figuring out his role in all of it.

 More observations: 

 
 Even though Josh Sweat hasn't practiced this camp and there isn't a set timeline for his return, defensive coordinator Nick Rallis said Tuesday that Sweat is "locked in" with meetings and post-practice tape. 
 

 
 Aug. 3 
 Deep balls were the theme of the day for the Cardinals as Jacoby Brissett ,  Gardner Minshew II  and Carson Beck put on an aerial display.

 Brissett unleashed a bomb to Marvin Harrison Jr ., who, after letting a deep ball earlier in practice go off his fingertips, came down with a diving grab that would have gained more than 50 yards.

 Beck showed off his deep ball, hitting fellow rookie Reggie Virgil on a beautiful pass. On another deep shot, Beck froze two defenders in the second level before finding a receiver who made the catch a step in front of a defender.

 More observations from the day:  

 
 Tight end Trey McBride was banged up briefly after he was hit in the middle of the field. He went down and was slow to get up but later returned to the offensive drills. 
 The tip drill paid off for the defense on two different plays Monday. On one, defensive lineman  Zachary Carter  tipped a pass by Minshew and L.J. Collier came down with it. On another play, defensive lineman  Roy Lopez  batted down a Beck pass. 
 The catch of the day came from Virgil, who made an impressive one-handed catch in mid-air as he was falling to the ground on a pass from Beck along the sideline. 
 

 

 Aug. 2 
 Jacoby Brissett continues to get more and more comfortable with the offense, as was evident Sunday.
 He had seven drives with the first-team offense, totaling 29 snaps, and finished 13-for-16 passing with two interceptions.

 The first was by defensive back Sean Murphy-Bunting , who jumped the route in front of Michael Wilson for the pick. The second was by second-year linebacker Cody Simon . Brissett's other incompletion was an overthrow.

 Overall, though, Brissett looked to be better in command of what's being asked of him. He didn't have a completion to Marvin Harrison Jr ., who was the intended target on Simon's interception, but Brissett did find a favorite receiver in tight end Trey McBride , who caught all six of the targets thrown his way.

 Back-up quarterback  Gardner Minshew II  was 9-for-13 passing and Carson Beck was 9-for-12 passing. While Beck wasn't consistent with his deep passes, he completed a couple of passes while he was off-balance, showcasing poise in the pocket.

 

 More observations from the day: 

 
 Second-year defensive lineman Walter Nolen III said the discomfort with his left knee during Friday's practice -- the same knee that ended his rookie season in 2025 -- was just a little hiccup. He said he wasn't concerned when it happened. He told himself he needed to slow down. 
 With the Cardinals' third block (every four days of practice is considered a block) of training camp starting Sunday, rookie running back Jeremiyah Love got the first snap of 11-on-11 with the first-team offense. Until Sunday, that was reserved for Tyler Allgeier . 
 Ihmir Smith-Marsette , who had been one of the surprise standouts of training camp thus far, left practice with a trainer and did not return. 
 Devin Duvernay , the lightning quick return specialist, showed he can be a factor as a receiver, as well. During the second-team, red zone 11-on-11, he caught a pass from Minshew on the right side, stopped in his tracks and reversed course to lose the defensive back and score a touchdown. 
 
 

 July 31 
 Cardinals rookie running back Jeremiyah Love showed off his highly lauded pass-catching ability on Friday in a play that also highlighted his quickness and shiftiness.

 During one of Arizona's 11-on-11 sessions, Love lined up in the backfield but then sidestepped to the right enough to take off from the slot at the snap. He then put a stutter step and a cut on second-year linebacker Cody Simon that left Simon in Love's dust. Love then cut inside and caught a pass from quarterback Jacoby Brissett .

 Even though it was a small sample size, Love is pleased with his role in the Cardinals' passing game thus far.

 "I like that they're trying to utilize me in ways that benefit me," he said. "I'm a guy that loves to get out in space. If I get out in space, I feel like I can make a play against whoever, whether it's linebacker, safety, I can…

title: 2026 Baltimore Ravens training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Follow our daily updates from Ravens training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The  Baltimore Ravens ' camp is taking place at Under Armour Performance Center in Baltimore, and Ravens reporter Jamison Hensley has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and of course the quarterback room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Ravens camp. We will update this file often. Can new coach Jesse Minter get  Lamar Jackson  and the Ravens to the Super Bowl? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive in to all the updates and be sure to check back for more information until the first full week of the preseason begins Aug. 13.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from Ravens camp 
 
 Zay Flowers, Ravens agree to four-year, $140M extension 
 Derrick Henry, entering 11th year, not thinking about retirement 
 Ravens waive rookie Diego Pavia to make room for Ethan Pocic 
 Ravens' Madubuike (neck) practices for 1st time in 10 months 
 
 
 Sunday, Aug. 9 
 Putting on full pads for the fourth time in training camp, the Ravens had one of their most physical practices of the summer. It was also their sloppiest.

 Baltimore's first, second and third offenses totaled eight false starts during the two-hour practice. The Ravens' starting offense jumped offside twice during a red-zone drill.

 Ravens coach Jesse Minter indicated the offense was trying to mix up the quarterback cadence on Sunday to keep the defense on its heels.

 "I think it's a great message of just the focus and the details that's required for that to become a real weapon and not something that puts you behind the chains like it did a few times today," Minter said.

 Other observations:  

 
 Just like he's done all camp, rookie wide receiver Ja'Kobi Lane had a couple more big plays, including working back to make a 15-yard grab in front of cornerback Marlon Humphrey . But Lane's most impressive play Sunday was his block on the perimeter that helped running back Derrick Henry gain some extra yards. 
 Minter reiterated that wide receiver Zay Flowers won't miss much time after leaving Saturday's practice with a quad contusion. "I feel good that he'll be back out there being Zay pretty soon," Minter said. 
 Safety Jaylinn Hawkins has made it difficult for wide receivers to go over the middle. On Saturday, Hawkins' collision with Flowers caused him to leave practice with a quad contusion. A day later, Hawkins crashed into Rashod Bateman to force an incompletion. Asked if there is a lesson for Hawkins to learn, Minter said, "I really don't want to put that on him. When you're a safety and you're breaking on the ball, there's just a little bit of an awareness of not trying to have the body-on-body collisions. We certainly want Jaylinn to play with the mindset that he plays with. So we'll continue to just be really, really careful about that." 
 Starting nose tackle Travis Jones "will be starting to work back in real, real soon," Minter said. Jones is on the Physically Unable to Perform list with a pectoral injury. Defensive end Calais Campbell participated in team drills for the first time in camp. Both Jones and Campbell should be ready for the Sept. 13 season opener. 
 Kicker Tyler Loop was 8-of-8 on field goal attempts, including three from beyond from 50 yards. Loop, whose missed 44-yard kick ended the Ravens' season, has been starting to hit a groove in camp. 
 
 

 Saturday, Aug. 8 

 On a day when  Zay Flowers ' injury scare headlined practice, wide receiver Ja'Kobi Lane continues to record one of the most impressive training camps by a Ravens rookie with more highlight-making receptions.

 Lane caught a deep touchdown pass from Lamar Jackson on a go route in a one-on-one drill against top cornerback Nate Wiggins and then made a one-handed catch on a back-shoulder throw by Tyler Huntley 25 yards down the field. After Lane's latest one-handed grab, running back Derrick Henry leapt in the air to give a shoulder bump to the impressive third-round pick.

 "There is consistency of making really contested, nice catches -- being a really friendly target for the quarterback," coach Jesse Minter said. "He's certainly starting to see a vision of maybe what he can become in the offense."

 Lane's strong camp has solidified a spot in Baltimore's three-wide formation, along with Flowers and Rashod Bateman .

 

 Other observations:  

 
 Running back Justice Hill called first-year playcaller Declan Doyle "the most detail-oriented" offensive coordinator that he's been with. In Hill's previous seven seasons, he's had two offensive coordinators: Greg Roman, who directed the NFL's highest-scoring offense in 2019, and Todd Monken, who guided Baltimore to the No. 1 offensive ranking in 2024. 
 The Ravens' defense got its hands on a lot of passes. T.J. Tampa , Malaki Starks and Amani Oruwariye all recorded pass breakups. Tampa is having an impressive camp and provides quality depth at cornerback behind Wiggins and Marlon Humphrey . 
 The best route of the day came from rookie tight end Josh Cuevas , who faked outside before running to the middle to shake free of safety Keondre Jackson for the easy catch. The Ravens are hoping for one of their rookie draft picks -- Cuevas and Matt Hibner -- to step up and provide another pass-catching target at tight end behind Mark Andrews . 
 The Ravens signed inside linebacker Jamon Johnson , a local product who attended St. Frances High School in Baltimore. He played in two games last season, making 10 tackles. The Ravens waived undrafted rookie cornerback Matthew McDoom to make room for Johnson on the 90-man roster. 
 

 

 Thursday, Aug. 6 
 The Ravens' third practice of the week in full pads was also their chippiest.

 The first dust-up of camp came when outside linebacker Tavius Robinson shoved offensive tackle Carson Vinson after the play. This caused the offensive and defensive players to converge in the middle of the field before they were quickly separated.

 There were no punches thrown, but coach Jesse Minter huddled the team together shortly afterward.

 "It was just a reminder of [how] the whole reason we are out here is to make each other better [and] help us get ready to play when we are playing against somebody else," Minter said.

 In what was the longest practice of camp at 2 1/2 hours, Minter intentionally scripted long drives of eight and nine plays, which can take a toll on a day when the heat index reached 92 degrees.

 "You want to be able to do all that with a high, high level of physicality and also keep your wits about you," Minter said.

 Other observations: 

 
 Ferran Torres, the star of the World Cup, watched practice and spoke to the players afterward. Torres came off the bench to score the winning goal in Spain's World Cup triumph. "Talk about just being ready when your number is called [and] being at your best when your best is needed -- that is like the ultimate," Minter said. 
 Kyle Hamilton showed why he is one of the best -- and most versatile -- safeties in the league. During team drills, Hamilton was constantly in the backfield and even recorded a sack of Lamar Jackson . Then, in one-on-ones, Hamilton intercepted Jackson after blanketing Elijah Sarratt on a fade route. 
 In one of the most hands-on drills the Ravens have ever had, Baltimore had its defensive backs work on tackling by hitting coaching interns. As Minter pointed out, the coaches were holding a pad and landed on a pad. "I think coaches will do anything to make players better, and we have a great group of coaches," Minter said. "All [of] those guys are willing to do whatever it takes."

full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The  Chicago Bears ' camp is taking place in Lake Forest, Illinois, and Bears reporter Courtney Cronin has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and, of course, the quarterbacks room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Bears camp. We will update this file often. Will the defense step up and lead the Bears back to the NFC North title? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive into all the updates and be sure to check back for more information until the first full week of the preseason begins Thursday.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest Bears news 
 
 Darnell Wright agrees to record deal 
 New Bears safety Coby Bryant out 8-10 weeks with injury 
 Bears CB Johnson views 2026 as 'definitely a contract year' 
 Ben Johnson: Bears motivated to spurn 'regression' label 
 
 
 Aug. 9 
 Practice No. 10 of training camp -- the Bears' fifth in pads -- moved indoors after a lengthy lightning delay and opened with physical, downhill run drills. D'Andre Swift has looked terrific through the first two weeks and was seemingly everywhere Sunday: in the run game, passing game and taking a direct snap during 11-on-11 reps.

 Swift picked up two big runs as the Bears repped their four-minute offense at the end of a two-hour session.

 Luther Burden III missed practice because of a groin injury and is expected to miss "a little bit of time," according to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport. In Burden's absence, Jahdae Walker had back-to-back solid practices and hauled in the best catch of the day from Caleb Williams on a busted-coverage deep ball.

 Defensive coordinator Dennis Allen worked in his dime package and emphasized blitzes/different pressures in 11-on-11 reps. Cornerback Tyrique Stevenson , who battled through injury during Saturday's practice, picked off Williams' pass on an out route to Rome Odunze .

 In addition to Burden, the Bears were also missing Cam Lewis , Montez Sweat , Braxton Jones , Jaylon Jones , D'Marco Jackson , Terell Smith and Coby Bryant .

 Rookie wide receiver Zavion Thomas appeared to injure his knee during 7-on-7 drills. He left practice with a trainer and did not return.

 Other observations:  

 
 Kiran Amegadjie got first-team reps at left tackle. The Bears continue to rotate Amegadjie and  Jedrick Wills Jr . at left tackle with the ones, twos and threes and have yet to get Theo Benedet in the mix. 
 Allen said he didn't think Lewis' injury would sideline the DB for long but did not have a timetable on his return. Lewis was injured Saturday as the Bears repped an end-of-game situation toward the end of practice. 
 Newly signed DB Xavier Woods filled in for Lewis at safety opposite rookie Dillon Thieneman . Woods laid a heavy hit on Colston Loveland over the middle and made a strong impression on his second day with the Bears. 
 Linebacker Ruben Hyppolite II had his best practice of training camp. He has been getting more reps in Jackson's absence. 
 The long-snapper competition appears to be over. Luke Elkin was waived Sunday before practice, leaving Beau Gardner as the sole long snapper on the 90-man roster. 
 Malik Muhammad continues to get a sizeable workload at nickel with the first-team defense. With Jaylon Jones sidelined and Josh Blackwell seemingly behind Muhammad on the depth chart, the rookie has stood out to coaches and shown signs of being able to hold his own at one of the most difficult positions for a young player. "The biggest challenge you've got is you got a big bull's-eye on your back and they're [opposing quarterbacks] going to be challenging you," Allen said. "They're going to be coming after you. The best corners have really short memories because everybody at some point in time has been beaten, and so it's just can you come back the next play and have the same mentality in terms of how you challenge and how you compete, and he's shown that he's got the ability to do that." 
 
 
 

 Aug. 8 

 The Bears were already without defensive end Montez Sweat , left tackle Braxton Jones and cornerback Jaylon Jones when they suited up for Saturday morning's padded practice. The injury hits kept coming during the 105-minute session.

 On the final rep of red zone one-on-ones, wide receiver  Luther Burden III and cornerback  Tyrique Stevenson got tangled up while the defensive back broke up a pass from Caleb Williams . Stevenson landed awkwardly on his back while Burden appeared to sustain a lower body injury.

 After several moment where Stevenson laid on the ground in visible pain, the cornerback was helped to his feet and received treatment on the sideline from a trainer, who rubbed ointment on the lower right side of his back. Stevenson fought through pain to finish practice despite having to pull himself out of an 11-on-11 period.

 Burden, on the other hand, walked gingerly toward the weight room under his own power flanked by a trainer. He did not return to practice.

 Chicago can't afford another injury to its secondary that has been without nickel corner Kyler Gordon (calf) all of training camp and lost safety Coby Bryant for an expected eight to 10 weeks Monday. Backup safety Elijah Hicks remains on the PUP list with a calf injury.

 Cam Lewis , who is filling in for Bryant at safety, left practice during the final period with an apparent leg injury. Lewis was guarding wide receiver Rome Odunze in the red zone when he got hurt and rode away on the back of a cart. Lewis was replaced by Skyler Thomas at safety.

 Other observations: 

 
 Jedrick Wills Jr . got first-team reps at left tackle with Braxton Jones sidelined. He struggled during OL/DL one-on-ones, getting beat twice and false starting once. 
 With Jaylon Jones sidelined, rookie Malik Muhammad was once again with the first-team defense at nickel. Muhammad broke up a pass during 11-on-11 and almost came away with an interception later. 
 Sixth-round defensive tackle Jordan van den Berg was a part of the rotation with the first-team defense during low red zone drills. He excelled with his bull rush against center Logan Jones during one-on-one drills. "I think he's going to be a hell of a football player," defensive tackle Neville Gallimore said. 
 Colston Loveland caught two touchdown passes from Williams while covered during 7-on-7. His second TD grab came in the corner of the end zone with a defender draped over him as he dove to catch the ball. 
 The focus at the end of practice was three end-of-game situations. Tyson Bagent dropped a dime into  Jahdae Walker 's hands on fourth down for a touchdown. Williams ended practice with an exclamation point when he bought time upon dropping back with 12 seconds on the clock before throwing a 17-yard laser to Odunze in the back of the end zone. Odunze caught the pass with multiple defenders around him. 
 

 

 Aug. 6 
 The longest practice of training camp to date was also the most physical. The Bears were in pads Thursday for 130 minutes and commenced team periods with old-school 9-on-7 and 9-on-9 running drills. With music blasting across the practice fields closest to Halas Hall, the physical, downhill running session turned up the temperature in practice between the offense and defense with a handful of shoving matches after plays were blown dead.

 "Shoot, we love it," defensive end Austin Booker said. "That's our mentality this year: We're getting off the ball, we're being aggressive and getting in the backfield."

 The intensity carried over to one-on-ones between the offensive and defensive lines. Two days after becoming the highest-paid right tackle in NFL history ( four years, $116 million ), Darnell Wright won all three of his reps taken against defensive end Montez Sweat .

title: Bears add new pieces to secondary, adjust on fly
summary: With injuries to Coby Bryant and Kyler Gordon, the Bears will try new faces and new wrinkles to hang tough.
full_text:
LAKE FOREST, Ill. -- Dennis Allen has been in problem-solving mode since the Chicago Bears opened training camp.

 Without Kyler Gordon , who was placed on the physically unable to perform list after what general manager Ryan Poles called "a delay" in his recovery from a calf injury, Allen was forced to find another player who could fill in indefinitely at nickel corner.

 For the first four days of camp, that concern appeared to be assuaged. Then came another.

 During one-on-one drills Aug. 3, safety Coby Bryant left practice because of a hyperextended left knee, bone bruise and small fracture. Though Bryant is not expected to need surgery, the recovery timetable is anywhere from eight to 10 weeks, a source told ESPN's Adam Schefter.

 Allen once again was in mitigation mode as he braced for the barrage of questions that came from the domino effect created by these injuries.

 Would Cam Lewis , who had been filling it at nickel, move to safety? Who now plays slot corner? What does Bryant's injury mean for rookie safety Dillon Thieneman ? What does he want to see out of Player X, Y, Z as he calls on players further down the depth chart?

 Allen aimed to answer every inquiry with one retort.

 "You know what I want to see?" Allen said. "I want to see 11 frickin' dudes on the field competing their ass off. And if we all do that, then I feel pretty confident that we'll get them to the right spot."

 Having to pivot and adjust to a rotating cast of defensive backs is hardly new for Allen, who enters his second season as the Bears' defensive coordinator. Allen has never had a training camp practice with all of his starters in the secondary healthy at the same time.

 In 2025, cornerback Jaylon Johnson was sidelined from camp because of a groin injury, while Gordon missed most of the preseason because of a soft tissue ailment. That's no different this camp. In addition to Gordon's and Bryant's injuries, the Bears' top backup safety, Elijah Hicks , opened camp on the PUP list. Lewis, who has since moved to safety to fill Bryant's spot, exited Saturday's practice during red zone drills because of a lower-body injury. Chicago lost two backup DBs -- Gervarrius Owens and Dallis Flowers -- to significant leg injuries.

 In need of reinforcements, the Bears signed 10-year veteran safety Xavier Woods and worked out nine defensive backs Friday, and that led them to sign William Wright and Brandon Hill .

 Bryant was Chicago's marquee free agent acquisition, having signed a three-year, $40 million deal weeks after winning Super Bowl LX with the Seattle Seahawks . The Bears banked on his speed and experience to elevate the secondary while simultaneously helping develop Thieneman, the No. 25 pick, who is just over a month from his first NFL start.

 

 For now, that job belongs to Lewis, whose versatility is his superpower. It's a trait that intrigued Chicago to sign him as a free agent after seeing what it provided the Buffalo Bills since 2020. Lewis rotated between positions in the secondary and played in 17 games, including 10 starts, in each of the past three seasons. He also appeared in 11 playoff games, with his first start coming against the Denver Broncos in the divisional round.

 "I've been doing cross-training, you would say, for a little bit of time now," Lewis said. "Honestly, my whole career. You try to get a grasp of the whole defense ... the concepts, teaching, how they want different positions to play. Say if it's at linebacker and we're playing Cover 3, how they play Cover 3 for a curl flat would be the same thing as a nickel.

 "Understanding the concept and turning my brain off is like -- OK, I'm not playing safety now. I'm playing nickel. Let's focus on nickel. OK, I'm going back to safety, let's turn the safety brain on. It's a little adjustment, especially with a new system coming from Buffalo. Been putting in the work. You've got to put in extra work, study a lot just to make sure you understand what they're asking you to do."

 How much time Lewis might have to miss could force Allen to have to shake up his plans once again. That's at least how the contingency has played out at nickel. Allen tabbed Jaylon Jones and Josh Blackwell , who have a combined seven in-game snaps at slot corner in this defense, along with rookie Malik Muhammad . But Jones, too, has been sidelined because of injury since Thursday.

 Muhammad, the fourth-rounder from Texas, has taken most of his reps with the first-team defense at nickel. The trial-by-fire experience has given the rookie a real-time education at one of the most complex positions on defense. During Saturday's practice, Muhammad broke up a pass in the red zone and almost had an interception in a later team period.

 The Bears' secondary cannot afford another injury, not if it plans to be the strength of this defense, as Poles forecasted in April.

 "In this situation where we have good corners, good safeties, we can be in a position where maybe we can have the quarterback hold the ball a little longer," Poles said April 23.

 Though still early, the next-man-up philosophy has already run through several cycles. Slowing that cycle is the key to establishing continuity within the secondary.

 "DA is still installing his defense schemes right now," coach Ben Johnson said. "We're still installing offense schemes. There's a lot of learning going on. And as we go through camp, we'll come to a consensus on the players we can count on most, who the starters will be, what role they're going to play and whether we'll adjust things schematically to have the most success on the field. That's what we do. We're not in panic mode by any stretch with some guys going down. That's what happens in this league. It's going to happen to every team throughout camp and throughout the season. We're no different than that."

title: 2026 Cincinnati Bengals training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Follow our daily updates from Bengals training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The Cincinnati Bengals ' camp is taking place in Cincinnati, and Bengals reporter Ben Baby has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and of course the quarterback room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Bengals camp. We will update this file often. Will Dexter Lawrence II spark a defensive resurgence to get the Bengals back in the playoffs? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive in to all the updates and be sure to check back for more information until the first full week of the preseason begins Aug. 13.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest Bengals stories 
 
 Joe Burrow, Bengals find camaraderie on unusual battlefield 
 Bengals DE Stewart out multiple weeks with hyperextended knee 
 Bengals' top storylines at training camp 
 

 

 Sunday, Aug. 9 
 Chalk it up to a good day for the offense. The first-team unit had some good moments on a Sunday afternoon that featured two extensive move-the-ball drills. One of them ended with a corner touchdown pass from Joe Burrow to Tee Higgins . The running game also had some moments, which is a good sign for an offense looking to find bigger gains on the ground.

 

 
 Bengals safety Bryan Cook and cornerback Dax Hill did not practice. Both have been battling muscle tightness in recent days. The indication on Cook, who suffered his injury in the team's Friday night practice, is that his issue is nothing significant. 
 

 
 Friday, Aug. 7 
 Cincinnati wants to find bigger gains in the ground game in 2026. There was a healthy amount of that in the limited portion of practice that was inside Paycor Stadium on Friday night.

 Running back Chase Brown reeled off a long run for a TD, which is a good sign for team that lacked explosive rushing plays last season. The Bengals were tied for 24th in the NFL in gains of 10 or more yards on the ground by running backs, according to ESPN Research.

 More observations: 

 
 The team spent the bulk of the practice at its indoor bubble because of thunderstorms that were in the area. They came back to Paycor Stadium for a few periods for the fans that stayed. 
 Safety Bryan Cook received some treatment from trainers after favoring his left hamstring. He didn't come back out with the first-team defense for its final drive. 
 Others who did not practice today: CB Dax Hill , CB Jalen Davis , DT Jonathan Allen  and WR Tee Higgins . Hill has been limited with muscle tightness the past few days. 
 DT  Dexter Lawrence II  knocked QB Joe Burrow to the ground during team drills inside the stadium. It was a light brush. 
 For a passing offense that has struggled at times in camp, it had a good moment inside the stadium. Burrow connected on a deep throw to WR  Ja'Marr Chase  behind the Cincinnati secondary. 
 
 
 Thursday, Aug. 6 
 The offensive tinkering continued on Thursday as the Bengals try to find different ways to put pressure on opposing defenses. Throughout training camp, Cincinnati has had a ton of reps with QB Joe Burrow under center, which is not typically how the Bengals like to operate. But it's clear that finding ways to mix up the offensive formations is a strategy that will be critical to creating a more explosive offense. And offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher is OK with any lumps that are taken during the process.

 "We just wanna have a lot of tools at our disposal," Pitcher said on Thursday. "And that's what we're developing right now."

 
 The offense and defense traded pre-snap victories during an unscripted 11-on-11 drill. First, the defense forced a delay of game. But the offense responded by drawing the defense offsides. 
 Rookie defensive end Cashius Howell continues to turn heads. Howell took reps with the first team and created pressure off the edge. The second-round pick has been one of the camp's biggest stars. 
 Cincinnati appears to be experimenting with its back-up offensive tackles. Cody Ford and Andrew Coker swapped between the left and right sides during second-team reps. Cincinnati is looking to solidify the swing tackle spot behind starters Orlando Brown Jr . and Amarius Mims . 
 

 

 Tuesday, Aug. 4 
 The defense continues its strong start to training camp. That was punctuated by a two-play exchange that started with a pass deflection by CB  DJ Turner  on a deep ball intended for WR Ja'Marr Chase , before safety S Bryan Cook had a pick-six off QB Joe Burrow during a team drill. Coordinator Al Golden's group has looked nothing like the team that has struggled in each of the past two seasons.

 "I think as a defense, we have an edge," Golden said. "We gotta continue to have that edge. We haven't done anything."

 
 Bengals CB DJ Ivey took first-team reps with Dax Hill sidelined. Hill was dealing with a bit of tightness and was limited for precautionary reasons. 
 DT Jonathan Allen was not at practice in what appeared to be a vet rest day. Allen also missed a day last week before quickly returning. 
 Cincinnati released S Isaiah Nwokobia on Tuesday. He had not practiced in back-to-back days. 
 

 

 Monday, Aug. 3 
 The first day of pads belonged to the Bengals' defense. And in what has become a recurring theme, the defensive line was able to bring some good pressure. Boye Mafe continued to affect the quarterback and rookie Cashius Howell had a clean win off the edge against the second-team defense.

 The defense isn't letting any camp success get to their heads. "We haven't scratched the surface, which is the encouraging thing," said linebacker Barrett Carter . "Our floor right now is high. I'm not trying to jinx us or put expectations on us, but we're stacking days, and we just have to keep doing that. We're nowhere near where we can be."

 More observations: 

 
 Dalton Risner and  Orlando Brown Jr . spent a good amount of time decompressing in the locker room talking about how the day went for them. It was a detailed conversation, which Risner said was an example of the group being dialed in this early in camp. 
 Rookie wide receiver Colbie Young made a couple of good catches. The coaching staff has been adamant that the fourth-round pick out of Georgia can carve out a role on this year's offense. 
 

 

 Saturday, Aug. 1 
 Have a day, Boye Mafe . The recent Super Bowl winner was disruptive throughout Saturday's practice. He consistently produced pressure against Joe Burrow and the first-team offense, including getting into a passing lane and forcing an interception .

 It has continued a good first week for the defense. But Mafe, who helped the Seahawks win the Lombardi Trophy in February with the Seahawks, knows Cincinnati has a long way to go.

 "I feel like we're really just setting our standard," Mafe said. "You can't mistake activity for achievement." 

 More observations: 

 
 WR Tee Higgins did not practice today but was a close observer. The team has made it a point to limit his workload to avoid any major soft-tissue injuries, a strategy that worked last season. 
 Former Bengals defensive end Sam Hubbard, who retired after the 2024 season, stopped by Saturday's practice to see his old teammates. 
 Practice started indoors because of rain but eventually moved to the outdoor fields. 
 Cornerback DJ Turner had a good pass deflection on a deep ball intended for Ja'Marr Chase . But was notable was the defensive backs making sure to yell "Ball!" to let Turner know the passes was about to arrive. It was an example of the communication the secondary has displayed during the first week of camp.

title: 2026 Dallas Cowboys training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Follow our daily updates from Cowboys training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The Dallas Cowboys ' camp is taking place in Oxnard, California, and Cowboys reporter Todd Archer has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and, of course, the quarterbacks room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at the Cowboys' camp. We will update this file often. Will Dallas turn around the NFL's worst defense from 2025? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive in to all the updates and be sure to check back for more information until the first full week of the preseason begins Aug. 13.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from Cowboys camp 
 
 Cowboys' Dak Prescott not shying away from setting lofty goals 
 Jones optimistic about Cowboys, likes 'what we put together' 
 Source: Ex-Cowboys QB Will Grier returns as offensive assistant 
 Quieter offseason has Cowboys focused on the right things 
 

 
 Sunday, Aug. 9 
 The Cowboys' practice had a little that would make coaches on defense and offense happy.

 To start, the defense controlled the line of scrimmage against the run and was able to keep the passing game in check. In the final two periods of team drills, the offense was able to respond.

 In between, there was plenty of talk back and forth in what was the most physical practice of training camp.

 "It's fire, man," receiver CeeDee Lamb said. "I embrace it. It was good to see our defense come out with that type of energy, that type of fire, that type of aggression early on. For us as an offense, it leaves us no choice but to bow down or fight back and get on top. And I know one thing about us, we won't bow down to nobody."

 Other observations:  

 
 Dak Prescott and Lamb connected on two deep passes, including one that would have been a touchdown of more than 50 yards after he was able to get a step on cornerback DaRon Bland . His first deep reception came when he got a step on Cobie Durant . 
 After a Jaydon Blue touchdown run to the edge, safety P.J. Locke was able to read Prescott's eyes perfectly and come up with the interception in the end zone on what looked like a 2-point play. Later, Shemar James intercepted Prescott, who was under pressure. 
 Safety Jalen Thompson (hip) returned to 11-on-11 drills for the first time in a few days. The hope is he will be good to go from now on and practice against the Rams on Tuesday. 
 On the first two plays of team, edge rushers Donovan Ezeiruaku and Rashan Gary blew up consecutive runs. Ezeiruaku got off the ball quick to get to Javonte Williams . Gary's physical play with Tyler Smith stymied a Blue run. 
 The Cowboys do not practice Monday. They next time they hit the field in pads will be Tuesday at the Rams' facility in Woodland Hills. 
 
 

 Saturday, Aug. 8 

 Practice was not very old when coach Brian Schottenheimer wanted to get a point across to the players.

 While in the middle of individual drills, he called the group together from both practice fields and appeared to light into the players, expletives and all. After the Cowboys were in pads for three straight practices, perhaps Schottenheimer wanted to remind the players that padless practice doesn't mean less effort.

 Whatever it was, the message was received.

 "[He was] just reminding us that we have to have a productive day," pass rusher Donovan Ezeiruaku said. "It was nothing that really happened. It just felt as though he needed to do that as the head coach, and that's what he did. I think we had a pretty good day."

 Said wide receiver  George Pickens , "Just pushing guys to be better."

 Other observations:  

 
 QB  Dak Prescott had a sharp day, completing 15 of 19 passes, including 5 of 6 in a red zone period that saw him throw touchdown passes to Jake Ferguson and Pickens. Ferguson and Pickens were able to use their size to their advantage to beat S P.J. Locke and CB  Shavon Revel Jr . 
 Jerry Jones made the long flight back from the Pro Football Hall of Fame on Friday night to be in attendance for Saturday's practice. 
 Schottenheimer spent most of the practice observing on the sideline as offensive coordinator Klayton Adams called the plays from behind the line of scrimmage. It's the second time Adams has called the plays. Schottenheimer's comfort level with the offensive staff has grown. 
 CeeDee Lamb had two touchdown catches, including one on a route where he was able to out-leverage CB DaRon Bland to the outside by quickly getting out of his break. On the second, he and Prescott connected on a perfect back-shoulder throw on Revel. 
 

 

 Friday, Aug. 7 

 After he was tossed from Tuesday's practice for throwing a punch, second-year edge rusher Donovan Ezeiruaku had a conversation with coach Brian Schottenheimer.

 Schottenheimer said it was a "long talk."

 "I just talked to him about [how] we're playing this the way you would play a game. And I said, 'For an incredible player, you run hot'; that's part of his edge," Schottenheimer said. "He's an incredible play-style guy. He plays the game the right way, but at the same time, we have to have a plan that when he gets hot and when he feels his temperature rising, what is the plan?

 "So he and I discussed a couple different options. I think we've got a good thing in place, but again, I don't want to take away the edge that he plays on. But you throw a punch, you've gone over the edge, therefore you're going to get ejected.

 Schottenheimer said Ezeiruaku's reaction was "great."

 In Thursday's practice, Ezeiruaku was as active as he has been, providing pressure off the edge. And he didn't throw a punch.

 
 Thursday, Aug. 6 
 With the Cowboys holding their Military Appreciation Day at training camp Thursday, Dak Prescott was presented with a gift from a fan.

 It was a Cowboys hat with a picture of his brother Jace on the side. At first, Prescott said he just thought it was a normal hat until he saw Jace, who died in 2020 . Prescott's Faith Fight Finish Foundation, which honors his brother as well as his mother, addresses mental health and suicide prevention.

 "That actually means a lot," Prescott said. "I wish I knew who did it because I would've said thank you. I just thought it was a hat. I didn't see it until I go with my daughters [after practice]. 
 
"It's badass."

 

 More observations: 

 
 Coach Brian Schottenheimer wanted to clarify the state of the left tackle competition. Tyler Guyton hasn't been named the starter yet, but Nate Thomas needs to up his level to make sure there is a competition. Guyton took part in Thursday's work with his right elbow taped after he didn't finish Tuesday's practice. Guyton and Thomas had false-start penalties leading to their departures for a play. 
 Tight end  Jake Ferguson is off to a strong start in camp. He and Prescott have had a clear connection on the intermediate and seam throws, and they connected four times Thursday with one completion coming on a "free" play when the defense jumped early that led to a decent gain. 
 Rookie LB Jaishawn Barham did not finish practice because of a groin injury. A source said it wasn't believed to be serious, and Barham was able to return to the field to watch the final parts of the workout. 
 It did not rise to the level of the Donovan Ezeiruaku punch, but cornerback Caelen Carson and rookie receiver Anthony Smith got into a tug-of-war and needed to be separated by teammates. It was brewing with both players after a particularly physical play early in team drills. 
 LB Curtis Robinson had a near interception of a Sam Howell pass down the seam to tight end Brevyn Spann-Ford , reaching high with his right hand to knock it down. The ball nearly fell into Robinson's lap as he landed on the ground.

title: 2026 Detroit Lions training camp: Latest intel, updates
